nm:statphys-karamata-uniform-convergence.why: Source claim: Mikosch Theorem 1.2.4 and Geluk and de Haan Theorem 1.3 state this uniform convergence theorem. The record has no use evidence, so I judged influence and application from the mathematics. Inference: the Potter bounds, Karamata's integral theorem and Tauberian theorems use it, so res, pra and rea are 3. The proof needs lim sup sets and the reverse Fatou inequality, so pro is 2.

review.conditions: The statement needs only measurability, positivity and pointwise slow or regular variation. It claims uniformity only on compact [c, d] in (0, ∞), and this is true for every index ρ. The case c = d = 1 gives K = 0 and is trivial.
review.prerequisites: Step s4 needs the reverse Fatou inequality for indicators below the integrable indicator of [−2K, 2K]. The Fatou–Lebesgue theorem (wd:Q5437947) gives this lim sup form. Translation invariance and measurability of h are concepts, and no result prerequisite is absent.
review.alignment: I read Mikosch p. 9 in the local copy. The text before Theorem 1.2.4 says that the convergence is uniform on each compact subset of (0, ∞). Case (b) needs local boundedness, but the record uses case (a) and the reduction of s1. The proof matches Geluk and de Haan Theorem 1.3 on pp. 4-5.
review.why: All 5 proof steps are valid, and all 4 application steps are correct. The proof is the measure argument of Geluk and de Haan. The worked example gives the exact uniform error 4/(27(x + 1)) on [1, 4], and I recomputed every number.

step_reviews.why: The identity f(λx)/f(x) − λ^ρ = λ^ρ(L(λx)/L(x) − 1) is correct, and λ^ρ ≤ max(c^ρ, d^ρ) on [c, d]. The function h(u) = log L(e^u) is measurable. Slow variation gives h(u + v) − h(u) → 0 for each v.
Every λ in [c, d] is e^v with |v| ≤ K. The bound |e^t − 1| ≤ e^|t| − 1 holds for all real t. Thus S(u) → 0 is sufficient for the slowly varying claim.
If S does not tend to 0, the definition of the supremum gives ε, u_n and v_n. The triangle inequality shows A_n ∪ B_n = J. Since m(J) = 2K, 1 of the 2 sets has measure at least K.

C_n = B_n − v_n lies in [−2K, 2K] and has the measure of B_n. All arguments stay above u_n − 3K ≥ b. Reverse Fatou with the integrable bound 1 on [−2K, 2K] gives m(lim sup A_n) ≥ K. Here K > 0, because K = 0 forces v_n = 0.

A point y* in the lim sup set lies in infinitely many A_n, so |h(u_n + y*) − h(u_n)| ≥ ε/2 infinitely often. This contradicts h(u + y*) − h(u) → 0 for the fixed shift y*. The second case is the same with w_n → ∞.

computation_reviews.why: I checked the algebra. F̄(λx)/F̄(x) = λ⁻²(λx + 1)/(λ(x + 1)) = λ⁻²(1 − (1 − 1/λ)/(x + 1)). Thus the error is (λ⁻² − λ⁻³)/(x + 1), and it is not negative for λ ≥ 1.
g'(λ) = λ⁻⁴(3 − 2λ), so the maximum on [1, 4] is at λ = 3/2 with g(3/2) = 4/27. The end values g(1) = 0 and g(4) = 3/64 are smaller. The supremum 4/(27(x + 1)) is correct.
F̄(39)/F̄(26) = 40·26³/(27·39³) = (40/27)(2/3)³ = 320/729. I recomputed this value with exact fractions in Python.
(2/3)² = 324/729, so the error is 4/729. At x = 26 the bound 4/(27(x + 1)) is also 4/729, so λ = 3/2 attains the supremum.

nm:statphys-karamata-representation.why: The record proves the Karamata representation in both directions and the form for regularly varying functions. No use evidence exists in the record, so I judge influence and use from the mathematics. The theorem is a base tool of regular variation theory and gives Potter bounds and much of extreme value theory. The only conditions are measurability and positivity, so hyp is 4. The proof needs Karamata's integral theorem and absolute continuity, so proof simplicity is 2. One source and one followed proof support the record, so confidence is medium.

review.conditions: The statement needs only a measurable L > 0 on [a, ∞). The converse needs ε measurable and bounded on bounded intervals, so the integral exists. Positivity of c follows from L > 0. Both directions are true as written, also the regularly varying form with δ(u) → ρ.
review.prerequisites: Step s1 needs Karamata's integral theorem with index 0 for local boundedness and b(x) → 1, and the record lists it. Step s2 needs the Lebesgue differentiation theorem and the fundamental theorem of calculus for absolutely continuous functions. Both are listed. The list is complete.
review.alignment: I checked Mikosch, EURANDOM Report 1999-013, p. 8 (PDF page 10). Theorem 1.2.1 and Remark 1.2.2 are there as the excerpt says. The source lets c be non-negative and puts no condition on ε. The alignment states the added conditions on ε and the regularly varying form. The followed proof is Theorem 1.5 of Geluk and de Haan, p. 8, with formula (1.14) on p. 7, as I confirmed.
review.why: Accept. All 5 proof steps are valid. All 5 application steps are correct. Step a3 states x > y ≥ 1, so the strict bound L(x)/L(y) < 1 is true. I recomputed L(6)/L(3) = 7/8 and F̄(6)/F̄(3) = 7/32 with exact fractions.

step_reviews.why: Valid. Karamata's integral theorem with α = 0 gives X, local boundedness and b(x) = x L(x)/F(x) → 1. F(x₁) > 0 because L > 0. So b is measurable and bounded on each [x₁, y], since b(x) ≤ y sup L/F(x₁).

Valid. F is absolutely continuous, and F' = L a.e. by the Lebesgue differentiation theorem. log is Lipschitz on [F(x₁), ∞), so log F is absolutely continuous. Its derivative is L/F = b(s)/s a.e., and the fundamental theorem of calculus gives the integral formula.

Valid. L = bF/x, F(x) = F(x₁) exp(∫ b/s) and 1/x = (1/x₁) exp(−∫ ds/s) give the stated form on [x₁, ∞). The choice c = L and ε = 0 on [a, x₁) keeps the form for all x ≥ a. The limit c₀ = F(x₁)/x₁ is positive.
Valid. For x ≥ a·max(1, 1/λ) both x and λx lie in [a, ∞). The ratio c(λx)/c(x) tends to 1 because c₀ > 0. The integral is at most sup{|ε(u)| : u ≥ min(x, λx)} · |log λ|, and this tends to 0.

Valid. x^(−ρ) f(x) is slowly varying. The identity x^ρ = a^ρ exp(∫_a^x ρ/u du) moves ρ into the integrand, and a^ρ c(x) → a^ρ c₀ > 0. The converse uses ∫_x^{λx} ρ/u du = ρ log λ and the estimate of step s4 for δ − ρ.

computation_reviews.why: Correct. log L(x) = log(x + 1) − log 2 − log x, so x (log L)'(x) = x/(x + 1) − 1 = −1/(x + 1). This ε is continuous, |ε| ≤ 1/2 on [1, ∞), and ε(x) → 0.

Correct. For u ≥ y, −1/(y + 1) ≤ −1/(u + 1) < 0. For x > y the integral lies in [−log(x/y)/(y + 1), 0), so (y/x)^(1/(y+1)) ≤ L(x)/L(y) < 1. At y = 3 and x = 6 the lower bound is (1/2)^(1/4).
Correct. F̄(6)/F̄(3) = (7/432)/(4/54) = 7/32, and this equals (1/4)(7/8). The bounds of step a3 put it between (1/4)(1/2)^(1/4) ≈ 0.210 and 1/4. The value 7/32 ≈ 0.219 lies there.

nm:statphys-karamata-characterization.why: Source claim: Geluk and de Haan Theorem 1.2 states the characterization theorem. The record has no use evidence, so I judged influence and application from the mathematics. Inference: it shows that ratio limits must be powers of λ, and the theory of regular variation starts from it. The hypothesis is very weak, so hyp is 4. Steinhaus' theorem and the Cauchy equation give pro 2.

review.conditions: The statement needs a measurable f and a measurable set Λ of positive measure. Both conditions are necessary, as the 2 limitations of the record show. The conclusion g(λ) = λ^ρ on Λ follows from the limit for every λ > 0.
review.prerequisites: Steps s3 and s5 use Steinhaus' theorem (wd:Q3527166) for sets of positive measure. Step s1 uses the change of variables formula for λ ↦ log λ on E ⊂ [1/n, n]. Both prerequisites give exactly what the steps use.
review.alignment: I read pp. 3-4 of Geluk and de Haan in the local copy. The source proof uses F(t) = log f(e^t), Steinhaus' theorem and equation (1.7). It then uses Lusin's theorem for the last step. The alignment field says correctly that the record uses Steinhaus' theorem there.
review.why: All 6 proof steps are valid, and all 4 application steps are correct. The record also proves 2 facts that the source only states: K is a subgroup, and φ is measurable. The counterexample 2^⌊log₂ t⌋ in step a4 is correct.

step_reviews.why: For λ in Λ, h(u + log λ) − h(u) → log g(λ), so log Λ ⊂ K. On E = Λ ∩ [1/n, n], the change of variables gives m(log E) = ∫_E λ⁻¹ dλ ≥ m(E)/n > 0.
The 2 bracket decompositions are exact identities. Each bracket converges because u + w → ∞ and u − v → ∞. Thus K is closed under sums and negatives, and φ is additive on K.
log Λ has positive measure by step s1, so Steinhaus' theorem gives (−δ, δ) ⊂ log Λ − log Λ ⊂ K. Each real v is a sum of N copies of v/N in K. Thus K = ℝ.

Each φ_n is measurable because h is measurable and a translation keeps measurability. For fixed v, n + v ≥ log a for large n, and φ_n(v) → φ(v) along the integers. A pointwise limit of measurable functions is measurable.
The sets E_N increase to [0, 1], so 1 of them has positive measure. Steinhaus' theorem gives |φ| ≤ 2N on (−η, η). Then |φ(x) − xφ(1)| ≤ (2N + |φ(1)|η)/q for every q ≥ 1, so φ(x) = xφ(1).
With h(u) = log f(e^u), f(λt)/f(t) = exp(h(log t + log λ) − h(log t)). The exponent tends to φ(log λ) = ρ log λ. Thus f(λt)/f(t) → λ^ρ for every λ > 0.

computation_reviews.why: Λ = [1, 2] is measurable with measure 1, and the limits exist on it by assumption. The theorem gives 2^ρ = g(2) = 1/8, so ρ = −3.
3/2 lies in Λ = [1, 2], so g(3/2) = (3/2)⁻³ = 8/27. I recomputed this value in Python.
The theorem gives the limit for every λ > 0, also outside Λ. At λ = 10 the limit is 10⁻³ = 1/1000.
f(2t) = 2f(t) for every t ≥ 1, so the limit exists on the null set {2^k}. f(3t/2)/f(t) is 1 at t = 2^n and 2 at t = 3·2^(n−1). Thus no limit exists at λ = 3/2.

nm:statphys-karamata-integral-theorem.why: The record states and proves Karamata's theorem for all 3 index cases and both forms of the converse. No use evidence exists in the record, so I judge influence and use from the mathematics. The theorem is a standard tool for tail integrals, mean excess functions and moments of heavy tails. The converse needs a ratio limit, so hyp is 3. The proof needs the uniform convergence theorem, dyadic blocks and absolute continuity, so proof simplicity is 2. One source with its proof supports the record, so confidence is medium.

review.conditions: The direct part needs only a measurable, positive, regularly varying f. The case α = −1 has the correct o-relations, with the tail form only when ∫_X^∞ f < ∞. The converse needs a limit c ∈ (0, ∞), which gives index c − 1 > −1 or −c − 1 < −1. All parts are true as written.
review.prerequisites: Steps s1, s2 and s7 use the uniform convergence theorem, which the record lists. Step s8 uses the Lebesgue differentiation theorem and the fundamental theorem of calculus for absolutely continuous functions. Both are listed. Steps s3 to s6 use only pointwise regular variation. The list is complete.
review.alignment: I checked Geluk and de Haan, CWI Tract 40, p. 5 (PDF page 11). The excerpt matches Theorem 1.4. The proof on pp. 5-7 has the dyadic blocks, (1.10), (1.11) and (1.14). The alignment correctly names the separate case α = −1 and the direct integration in step s8.
review.why: Accept. All 8 proof steps are valid. All 4 application steps are correct. I recomputed ∫_9^∞ F̄ = 19/324, F̄(9) = 5/729 and e(9) = 171/20 with exact fractions. The ratio 19/20 matches (2u + 1)/(2u + 2) at u = 9.

step_reviews.why: Valid. The uniform convergence theorem on [1, 2] gives |f(λt)/f(t) − λ^α| ≤ 1, so the ratio is at most 2^|α| + 1. A chain along the points 2^k X gives f ≤ M^(n+1) f(X) on each dyadic block. A bounded measurable f is integrable on bounded intervals.

Valid. For x ≥ X/min(1, λ) both x and λx are at least X. The substitution s = xu is correct. Uniform convergence of f(xu)/f(x) on the compact u-interval between 1 and λ lets the limit pass inside the integral.
Valid. 2^α > 1/2 when α > −1, so f(2s) ≥ f(s)/2 for large s. The substitution gives I_n ≥ I_(n−1), so F(2^(n+1) s₀) ≥ (n + 1) I₀ with I₀ > 0. F is monotone, so F(x) → ∞.

Valid. The choice t₁ ≥ X/λ keeps λt₁ in the domain. The 2-sided pointwise bound puts F(λx) between F(λt₁) + (1 ∓ ε)λ^(α+1)(F(x) − F(t₁)). Division by F(x) → ∞ and then ε → 0 give F(λx)/F(x) → λ^(α+1).
Valid. (∗) with λ = 2 gives the limit (2^(α+1) − 1)/(α + 1) > 0, and step s4 gives the limit 2^(α+1) − 1 > 0. Their quotient is x f(x)/F(x), and it tends to α + 1.
Valid. 2^α < 1/2 for α < −1, so η exists and J_n ≤ 2η J_(n−1) with 2η < 1. Thus G is finite. For x ≥ t₁ the bound (1 ∓ ε)λ^(α+1) G(x) on G(λx) is exact. The quotient of the 2 limits gives −α − 1.
Valid. F(x) ≥ F(x) − F(x/K), and (∗) with λ = 1/K gives the limit log K. So lim sup x f(x)/F(x) ≤ 1/log K for every K > 1. The tail case uses G(x) ≥ F(Kx) − F(x) in the same way.

Valid. F is absolutely continuous with F' = g a.e., and log F is absolutely continuous on [x₁, y]. The integral of b(s)/s over [x, λx] tends to c log λ. Then g = bF/x gives index c − 1. The tail case with −(log G)' = b/s gives index −c − 1.

computation_reviews.why: Correct. F̄ = x⁻² (1 + 1/x)/2 is measurable and regularly varying with α = −2 < −1. Case (iii) gives ∫_u^∞ F̄ ~ u F̄(u)/(−α − 1) = u F̄(u). So e(u) ~ u.
Correct. F̄(s) = 1/(2s²) + 1/(2s³), so ∫_u^∞ F̄ = 1/(2u) + 1/(4u²) = (2u + 1)/(4u²). Division by (u + 1)/(2u³) gives u(2u + 1)/(2(u + 1)). The ratio e(u)/u tends to 1.
Correct. (171/20)/9 = 19/20, and (2 · 9 + 1)/(2 · 9 + 2) = 19/20. So the exact mean excess is 5% below the first-order value 9.

No use evidence exists in the record, so I judge influence and use from the mathematics. Potter bounds are the standard domination tool for integrals of regularly varying functions, for example in Tauberian proofs and Breiman's lemma. Any measurable regularly varying f is allowed, so hyp is 4. With the representation theorem the proof is short and elementary, so proof simplicity is 3. The evidence is one source, so confidence is medium.

step_reviews.why: Valid. The representation record gives f(x) = c(x) exp(∫_a^x η(u)/u du) with c → c₀ ∈ (0, ∞) and η → ρ. The quotient f(y)/f(x) then has the stated form, with an oriented integral when y < x.

Valid. Products of the bounds of steps s2 and s3 give the 2 inequalities. With A = 1 + ε/2 and δ = ε, A < 1 + ε and A⁻¹ ≥ 1 − ε/2 > 1 − ε. For λ ≥ 1 the max is λ^(ρ+ε) and the min is λ^(ρ−ε).

Correct. F̄(20) = 21/16000 and F̄(10) = 11/2000. The quotient is 21/88, as I recomputed with exact fractions.
Correct. (10/11)/4 = 5/22 = 20/88 and (11/10)/4 = 11/40 = 24.2/88. The value 21/88 lies between them. These are the δ-free bounds of step a2.
Correct. With y = 10x ≥ 10 the upper bound of step a2 gives at most (11/10) · 10⁻² = 11/1000. The exact quotient is (10x + 1)/(1000(x + 1)) < 1/100, so the bound holds.

nm:statphys-pollaczek-khinchine-ruin.why: Kyprianou (p. 4) calls the formula a cornerstone of insurance risk theory and the base of a large literature. This source claim sets research influence to 4. No use records exist, so practical impact and reach come from the mathematics. The formula gives exact ruin probabilities and, by duality, the M/G/1 waiting time law. The proof needs Fubini, Lebesgue differentiation and monotone convergence, so proof simplicity is 2. A general claim law needs convolution powers, so application simplicity is 2.

review.conditions: Each condition is correct. Poisson arrivals, i.i.d. positive claims with finite mean and ρ < 1 are the hypotheses of Kyprianou Theorem 1.3. The ruin event is a strict fall below 0 at some t > 0, as for τ_0^−.
review.prerequisites: The 5 prerequisites cover the steps. Fubini supports s1, s3 and s5. Lebesgue differentiation supports s2, and the fundamental theorem of calculus supports s3. The strong law and monotone convergence support s4.
review.alignment: The excerpt of Kyprianou Theorem 1.3 matches the statement with η = F_I and P_x(τ_0^− < ∞) = ψ(x). The alignment correctly says that the ψ form and ψ(0) = ρ are additions. It also says correctly that the proof is the renewal argument of Bingham.
review.why: All 5 proof steps and all 5 application steps are correct. The renewal equation, the value φ(0) = 1 − ρ and the remainder bound ρ^(n+1) are valid. The exponential example gives ψ(12) = 0.1128, and a direct sum of the series confirms it.

step_reviews.why: The reserve increases between claims, so ruin can occur only at a claim time. Survival from x is the event Z + V ≥ 0. Independence of V and (W₁, ξ₁) gives φ(x) = E φ(Z). The substitution s = x + ct is correct.
φ is nondecreasing, so h is a nondecreasing Borel function with values in [0, 1]. A is absolutely continuous with A' = −e^(−λx/c) h a.e. The product rule then gives φ' = (λ/c)(φ − h) a.e.
The fundamental theorem of calculus for the absolutely continuous φ gives the integral identity. Fubini gives ∫_0^t h = ∫_0^t φ(z) F(t − z) dz, because F(0) = 0. The renewal form follows from 1 − F.
The step mean c/λ − μ is positive because ρ < 1. The strong law makes V finite a.s., so φ(t) → 1. Monotone convergence in s3 then gives 1 = φ(0) + ρ.
The measure (λ/c)(1 − F(y)) dy equals ρ dF_I(y). After n iterations the remainder is in [0, ρ^(n+1)] and tends to 0. F_I has no atom at 0, so ψ(0) = (1 − ρ) Σ_{k≥1} ρ^k = ρ.

computation_reviews.why: ρ = 10 · 1/12 = 5/6. This value is less than 1, so the net profit condition holds and the theorem applies to the inputs.
For F(y) = 1 − e^(−y) and μ = 1, the integrated tail is 1 − e^(−x). The k-fold convolution of Exp(1) is Gamma(k, 1) with the stated Erlang tail.
All terms are nonnegative, so the exchange of sums is valid. The inner sum (1 − ρ) Σ_{k≥j+1} ρ^k equals ρ^(j+1). The result is ρ e^(−(1−ρ)x).
1 − 5/6 = 1/6, so ψ(x) = (5/6) e^(−x/6). At x = 0 this gives 5/6 = ρ, which agrees with the theorem.
(5/6) e^(−2) = 0.112779. A direct numerical sum of the PK series with Erlang tails also gives 0.112779. So the value 0.1128 is correct.

nm:statphys-embrechts-veraverbeke.why: Source claim: Zachary, arXiv:1410.8551, says that the theorem has well-known applications in queueing and risk theory. Mikosch calls relation (2.11) an elegant solution to the ruin problem for subexponential distributions. No use records exist, so practical impact and reach come from the mathematics. The proof needs the Pollaczek–Khinchine series, Kesten's bound and dominated convergence, so pro is 2. A use needs only ρ and the integrated tail, so app is 3.

review.conditions: The hypotheses are the Cramér–Lundberg model with positive claims and finite mean, the net profit condition ρ < 1, and subexponentiality of F_I. The condition is on F_I, not on F, as the original theorem requires. The condition ρ < 1 lets the proof choose ε with (1 + ε)ρ < 1 in step s3.
review.prerequisites: nm:statphys-pollaczek-khinchine-ruin gives the series for ψ under the same model and ρ < 1. F_I is a law on [0, ∞) with a positive tail. Thus nm:statphys-subexponential-convolution-tails gives parts (c) and (d) for F_I. Dominated convergence for the counting measure gives step s4. The record lists all prerequisites that the steps need.
review.alignment: Zachary Theorem 1(ii) states P(M > x)/F̄^s(x) → 1/a for a walk with mean −a. With a = c/λ − μ and F̄^s(u) ∼ μ(1 − F_I(u)), this gives ρ/(1 − ρ). The alignment text states this translation and the transfer of subexponentiality. It also states that the proof follows Mikosch, relations (2.8) to (2.11).
review.why: All 4 proof steps and all 5 application steps are correct. The proof is the classical argument of Embrechts and Veraverbeke. Kesten's bound gives a summable majorant that does not depend on u. The record states that it does not prove the converse.

step_reviews.why: G(u) > 0 by the definition of subexponentiality. The Pollaczek–Khinchine record gives ψ(u) = (1 − ρ) Σ_{n≥1} ρ^n (1 − F_I^{*n}(u)) under the same hypotheses. Division by G(u) is valid.
Part (c) of the linked lemma gives a_n(u) → n for n ≥ 2, and a_1(u) = 1. F_I is a law on [0, ∞) with a positive tail, so the lemma applies.
Part (d) of the linked lemma gives a_n(u) ≤ K(1 + ε)^n for all n ≥ 1 and u ≥ 0. Because 1 − ρ ≤ 1, each term is at most K((1 + ε)ρ)^n. This bound is summable because (1 + ε)ρ < 1.
Dominated convergence for the counting measure applies with the summable bound of step s3. The sum Σ nρ^n = ρ/(1 − ρ)², so the limit is ρ/(1 − ρ). I checked the identity ρ/((1 − ρ)μ) = λ/(c − λμ).

computation_reviews.why: ρ = λμ/c = (1/2)/(5/8) = 4/5. I recomputed the value 0.8. Thus the net profit condition ρ < 1 holds.
∫_u^∞ (1 + y)^(−3) dy = (1 + u)^(−2)/2. Multiplication by μ⁻¹ = 2 gives (1 + u)^(−2). This tail is regularly varying with index −2, so F_I is subexponential.
(4/5)/(1/5) = 4, and I recomputed this value. Thus ψ(u) ∼ 4(1 + u)^(−2) as u → ∞.
4/101² = 4/10201 = 3.92 · 10^(−4). The record rounds this value to 3.9 · 10^(−4), which is correct.
For exponential claims with mean 1/2, ψ(u) = ρ exp(−(1 − ρ)u/μ) = (4/5)e^(−2u/5). Then ψ(100) = 0.8 e^(−40) = 3.4 · 10^(−18). The ratio is 1.15 · 10^14, so the factor of about 10^14 is correct.

nm:statphys-brownian-ruin.why: The formula is the closed form of ruin for the diffusion approximation of a surplus. Moerters and Peres give it as Exercise 2.16 with a solution on p. 368. No use records exist, so influence and use come from the mathematics. The proof needs an exponential martingale, optional stopping and the limit B_t/t = 0. The application is direct with 3 inputs, so application simplicity is 4.

review.conditions: The conditions x > 0, µ > 0 and σ > 0 are correct and complete. For µ ≤ 0 the probability is 1, and the limitations of the record state this. τ is the first zero of a continuous surplus.
review.prerequisites: Optional stopping, the strong law, Markov, Borel–Cantelli and dominated convergence give what the steps use. The Doob record states the weak-type maximal inequality. Step s3 uses the L² form, which is a standard corollary.
review.alignment: Exercise 2.16 of Moerters and Peres gives P(B hits a + bt) = e^(−2ab). With −B, a = x/σ and b = µ/σ this is exp(−2µx/σ²). The proof follows the solution on p. 368 and adds the limit on {τ = ∞}, as the alignment says.
review.why: All 4 proof steps and all 4 application steps are correct. A small doubt is in s3. The cited Doob record states the weak form, not the L² form. The weak form for B² gives P(Y_0 ≥ εn) ≤ 1/(ε²n²) directly, so the step stays valid.

step_reviews.why: Gaussian increments give E[exp(λ(B_t − B_s)) | F_s] = exp(λ²(t − s)/2). With λ = −θσ, λ²/2 = 2µ²/σ² = θµ. So M_t = exp(−θ(X_t − x)) is a positive martingale with M₀ = 1.

τ is the first hit of a closed set by a continuous adapted process, so it is a stopping time. X ≥ 0 up to τ gives 0 < M_(t∧τ) ≤ e^(θx). Optional stopping at the bounded time t ∧ τ gives E M_(t∧τ) = 1.
The strong law gives B_n/n → 0. Doob's L² inequality gives E Y₀² ≤ 4, and the weak form for B² also gives the needed tail bound. Markov and Borel–Cantelli give Y_n ≤ εn eventually, so B_t/t → 0.
On {τ = ∞}, X_t/t → µ > 0 by s3, so M_(t∧τ) → 0. On {τ < ∞}, M_(t∧τ) = e^(θx) after τ. Dominated convergence with the constant bound gives 1 = e^(θx) P(τ < ∞).

computation_reviews.why: θ = 2 · (1/2)/4 = 1/4. The inputs µ = 1/2 and σ = 2 are positive, so the theorem applies for every x > 0.
The theorem gives ψ(x) = e^(−x/4). For x = 10, e^(−2.5) = 0.0821, so ψ(10) ≈ 0.082 is correct.
e^(−(x+y)/4) = e^(−x/4) e^(−y/4), so ψ is multiplicative. x₀ = 4 ln 10 = 9.21 gives ψ(x₀) = 1/10, and ψ(3x₀) = 1/1000.
ψ(x) ≤ 1/1000 exactly when x ≥ 4 ln 1000 = 12 ln 10 = 27.63. With σ = 4, θ = 1/16, so the capital is 16 ln 1000, which is 4 times larger.

nm:statphys-ladder-height-cramer-lundber.why: The result gives the law of the first ladder height. It is the base of the ladder height proof of the PK formula and of the deficit at ruin. Durrett derives it as formula (5.8.2). No use records exist, so influence and use come from the mathematics. The proof needs walk reversal, ladder heights and Tonelli. An application is one integral of the claim tail.

review.conditions: The conditions are correct. Poisson arrivals give the exponential right tail of the steps in s2, and the record says that they are necessary. Nonnegative claims with finite mean and ρ < 1 are sufficient.
review.prerequisites: The strong law makes T̄ finite in s3. Tonelli supports the exchanges of sums and integrals in s3, s4 and s5. Walk reversal and the strong Markov property of the walk are elementary facts without a separate record.
review.alignment: Durrett Example 5.8.15 proves (5.8.2) for a walk with exponential interarrival steps of rate α. With η = Y, ζ = cE and α = λ/c this walk is the claim surplus at claim times. The alignment is correct, and s5 does the integration of (5.8.2).
review.why: All 5 proof steps and all 4 application steps are correct. The integrated form in s5 agrees with the classical ladder height density (λ/c) B̄(y). The uniform claim example gives 4/5, 1/5, 1/4 and 2/3 correctly.

step_reviews.why: S decreases between claims, so τ₊ is a claim time and S(τ₊) = S_T. The sum c(E₁ + ⋯ + E_n) has a density, so P(S_n = 0) = 0 for n ≥ 1. Thus T = τ a.s., and the two probabilities are equal.
For x ≥ 0 and y ≥ 0, P(cE > x + y) = e^(−α(x+y)). Integration over B(dy) gives a e^(−αx) with a = ∫ e^(−αy) B(dy). This is Lemma 5.8.13 of Durrett.
On {T̄ > n − 1}, the tail of s2 gives P(T̄ = n, S̄_n > x) = e^(−αx) P(T̄ = n). So the ladder heights are i.i.d. Exp(α). The Gamma(k, α) densities sum to α, so the sum is αw.
Reversal of i.i.d. increments maps {S̄_1 > 0, …, S̄_n > 0} to a strict ascending ladder epoch at n. So ψ = δ₀ + α times Lebesgue measure. The last step and Tonelli give formula (5.8.2).
The formula g(u) = E[1{Y > u}(1 − e^(−α(Y−u)))] is correct. Tonelli gives α ∫_z^∞ g = α E(Y − z)⁺ − g(z). The sum is (λ/c) ∫_z^∞ B̄, and its continuity in z gives the strict form.

computation_reviews.why: ρ = 1 · 1/(5/4) = 4/5 < 1, so the theorem applies. With zero reserve, ruin is the event τ₊ < ∞, and its probability is ρ = 4/5.
Here λ/c = 4/5. The integral ∫₁² (1 − y/2) dy = 1 − 3/4 = 1/4. The product is 1/5, and the expression gives 0.2.
(1/5)/(4/5) = 1/4. The conditional density (λ/c) B̄(y)/ρ = B̄(y)/µ_B = 1 − y/2 integrates to 1 on [0, 2].
E Y² = 4/3 for the uniform law on [0, 2], so E Y²/(2µ_B) = 2/3. The direct integral ∫₀² y(1 − y/2) dy = 2/3 confirms the value.

nm:statphys-lindley-representation.why: The Lindley recursion is the base of the analysis of the G/G/1 queue. Gallager uses it to apply random walk threshold bounds to queue delay. No use records exist, so influence and use come from the mathematics. Parts (i) to (iii) hold for every i.i.d. law, so hypothesis burden is low. The proof is elementary. The law of M needs extra work, so application simplicity is 3.

review.conditions: Parts (i) to (iii) need only i.i.d. increments, and the record states this. Part (iv) needs E|U₁| < ∞ and E U₁ < 0, which the record lists. In the queue sentence, W₀ = 0 is the empty system at time 0.
review.prerequisites: The strong law of large numbers is the only result that a step needs, in s4 for S_k/k → E U₁ < 0. Steps s1 to s3 use only induction, invariance under permutation and continuity of measure.
review.alignment: Gallager Theorem 7.2.1 gives the maximum formula (7.6), the threshold probability by trial n and its limit. The record adds the form S_n − min S_i and part (iv). The alignment says this correctly, and footnote 4 supports the convergence in distribution.
review.why: All 4 proof steps and all 4 application steps are correct. The example gives P(W₃ ≥ 1) = 11/27 and the geometric limit law P(W ≥ k) = 2^(−k). An exact enumeration of the 8 paths confirms 11/27.

step_reviews.why: The induction is correct. W_(n−1) + U_n adds U_n to each window sum, and the maximum with 0 adds the empty window. The identity U_(n−k+1) + ⋯ + U_n = S_n − S_(n−k) gives the second form.
W_n = g(U_n, …, U₁) follows from s1. The product law of (U₁, …, U_n) does not change under reversal of the order. So W_n and M_n have the same law.
M_n increases to M, so {M_n > x} increases to {M > x}. Also {M_n ≥ x} increases to the event that some S_k ≥ x. Continuity from below and s2 give both limits.
The strong law gives S_k → −∞ a.s., so M is the maximum of finitely many finite terms. P(W_n ≤ x) → P(M ≤ x) at every real x, and M is finite a.s. So W_n converges in distribution.

computation_reviews.why: U = (2 − 1, 2 − 1, 2 − 3) = (1, 1, −1). The recursion gives W = (1, 2, 1). The window sums for n = 3 are 0, −1, 0 and 1, with maximum 1.
M₃ < 1 exactly when U₁ = −1 and (U₂, U₃) ≠ (1, 1). This event has probability (2/3)(8/9) = 16/27. So P(W₃ ≥ 1) = 11/27, and an enumeration confirms it.
(1/3)2^(s+1) + (2/3)2^(s−1) = 2^s. The walk has ±1 steps, so it hits k or −m exactly. The bounded stopped martingale gives the stated probability, with limit 2^(−k).
Part (iii) gives P(W ≥ k) = 2^(−k), so E W = Σ_(k≥1) 2^(−k) = 1. P(W₁ ≥ 1) = P(W₂ ≥ 1) = 1/3 is correct, and the limit is 1/2.

nm:statphys-spitzer-identity.why: Source claim: Kingman (1962) Lemma 1 quotes Spitzer's identity in a Banach algebra form. His Section 4 applies it to the reflected walk of the GI/G/1 queue. The record has no use evidence, so I judged influence and application from the mathematics. Inference: the identity is a base of fluctuation theory, the Sparre Andersen law and transform methods for queues, so res, pra and rea are 3. It needs only i.i.d. steps, so hyp is 4. The proof needs a Banach algebra, a projection and exponential series, so pro is 2. The application needs a homomorphism and a binomial series, so app is 2.

review.conditions: The statement needs only i.i.d. real steps and |x| < 1. No moment condition is necessary, because every g_n is a probability measure and the series converge in norm. The measure form and the characteristic function form are both correct.
review.prerequisites: Step s2 uses parts (i) and (ii) of nm:statphys-lindley-representation to give the reflected walk W_n the law of M_n. The other steps are Banach algebra arguments that the record proves in place. No result prerequisite is absent.
review.alignment: Kingman Lemma 1 on pp. 345-346 quotes the identity for a general projection P and gives no proof. Section 4 on p. 347 applies it to a walk with a barrier at 0, with g_(n+1) = P(f g_n). The alignment text states these facts and the restriction to ℝ correctly.
review.why: All 6 proof steps are correct. The projection P has the properties that Wendel's argument needs, and the factorization of δ₀ − x f into the 2 subalgebras is exact. The application gives the Sparre Andersen value 5/16, and a Monte Carlo check agrees.

step_reviews.why: Pµ is the image of µ under y ↦ max(y, 0), so P is linear, has norm at most 1 and satisfies P² = P. The range is the set of measures on [0, ∞). The kernel is the set of measures on (−∞, 0] with mass 0. Both are closed subalgebras with intersection {0}.
max(W_n + X_(n+1), 0) has the law P(g_n ∗ f), because X_(n+1) is independent of W_n. Parts (i) and (ii) of the Lindley record give W_n and M_n the same law. So g_n is the law of M_n.

G converges in norm because ‖g_n‖ = 1 and |x| < 1. Summation of g_(n+1) = P(f ∗ g_n) with weights x^(n+1) gives G − δ₀ = P(x f ∗ G). Then P(G ∗ A) = G − (G − δ₀) = δ₀, so G ∗ A − δ₀ is in the kernel of P.

The norm bound 1/(1 − |x|) makes the double series of exp(−L) absolutely convergent. So the scalar identity exp(log(1 − z)) = 1 − z transfers to x f. The algebra is commutative, so exp(−L) splits into exp(−PL) ∗ exp(−(I − P)L).

The left side is in the closed subalgebra 𝔐₊, which contains δ₀. The right side is δ₀ plus an element of the closed subalgebra 𝔐₋. The difference from δ₀ is in 𝔐₊ ∩ 𝔐₋ = {0}, so G = exp(PL). P f^(∗n) is the law of S_n⁺.

The map µ ↦ ∫ e^(iθy) µ(dy) is a bounded algebra homomorphism of 𝔐 into ℂ that sends δ₀ to 1. So it maps norm convergent series term by term and commutes with exp. This gives the characteristic function form.

computation_reviews.why: On measures carried by [0, ∞), y + z = 0 forces y = z = 0. So µ ↦ µ({0}) is a bounded homomorphism with value 1 at δ₀. Both sides are in 𝔐₊. Also P(M_n = 0) = P(S₁ ≤ 0, …, S_n ≤ 0) and P(S_n⁺ = 0) = P(S_n ≤ 0).
A symmetric atomless step law makes each S_n symmetric and atomless, so P(S_n ≤ 0) = 1/2. Then Σ xⁿ/(2n) = −(1/2) log(1 − x), and (1 − x)^(−1/2) = Σ C(2n, n)(x/4)ⁿ. The coefficients give C(2n, n)/4ⁿ.
C(6, 3) = 20 and 4³ = 64, so the value is 20/64 = 5/16. A Monte Carlo run with 400000 Gaussian walks gave 0.3122, close to 0.3125. The values for n = 1, 2, 3 are 1/2, 3/8 and 5/16.
Stirling's formula gives C(2n, n) ~ 4ⁿ/√(πn), so C(2n, n)/4ⁿ ~ 1/√(πn). The same value for all symmetric continuous laws is the Sparre Andersen theorem. The claim is correct.

nm:statphys-elementary-renewal.why: Source claim: Gallager Theorem 4.6.1 states the limit, and the text after the proof adds the infinite mean case. The record has no use evidence, so I judged influence and application from the mathematics. Inference: the theorem gives the mean renewal rate in reliability, insurance and queue models, so pra and rea are 3. It needs only i.i.d. positive steps, so hyp is 4. The proof needs Wald's equation and truncation, so pro is 3. The application divides by the mean, so app is 4.

review.conditions: The statement needs i.i.d. steps with P(ξ₁ > 0) = 1 and allows µ = ∞ with 1/∞ = 0. Both claims, m(t) < ∞ and m(t)/t → 1/µ, are true under these conditions. No arithmetic condition is necessary, and the record does not add one.
review.prerequisites: nm:statphys-wald-equation applies, because ν_t is a stopping time of the natural filtration with finite mean by step s1. Monotone convergence gives µ_c ↑ µ. The geometric series gives the bound K ε^(−K). The record lists all prerequisites that the steps need.
review.alignment: Gallager Theorem 4.6.1 on p. 191 states the limit. The proof on pp. 191-192 uses Wald's equation for the lower bound and truncation at b = √t for the upper bound. The record truncates at a fixed c and then lets c → ∞. The alignment text states these facts honestly.
review.why: All 5 proof steps and all 4 application steps are correct. The block argument in step s1 gives E ν_t ≤ K ε^(−K) without an extra exercise. The application value 599/4 and the second-order constant −1/4 are correct.

step_reviews.why: Strict positivity gives ν_t = 1 + N(t). A block of K steps above δ puts T_{jK} above Kδ ≥ t. Independence of the blocks gives P(ν_t > mK) ≤ (1 − ε^K)^m. The sum gives E ν_t ≤ K ε^(−K).
The event {ν_t = k} = {T_{k−1} ≤ t < T_k} depends only on ξ₁, …, ξ_k. Thus ν_t is a stopping time with finite mean. Wald's equation and T_{ν_t} > t give µ(1 + m(t)) > t. The case µ = ∞ is trivial.
T_{ν_t − 1} ≤ t and ξ_{ν_t} ≤ c give T_{ν_t} ≤ t + c. Wald's equation then gives µ E ν_t ≤ t + c. The step is correct.

The truncated steps are i.i.d., positive and bounded by c. T̄_k ≤ T_k gives ν̄_t ≥ ν_t. Steps s1 and s3 for the truncated steps give 1 + m(t) ≤ (t + c)/µ_c. Division by t gives the bound on the lim sup.
min(ξ₁, c) increases to ξ₁, so monotone convergence gives µ_c ↑ µ, also for µ = ∞. Thus lim sup m(t)/t ≤ 1/µ. Step s2 gives the lower bound 1/µ, so the limit is 1/µ.

computation_reviews.why: The Erlang law with shape 2 and rate 3 is strictly positive and has mean 2/3. Thus 1/µ = 3/2 per day, and m(100) ≈ 150 to first order.
T_k is the (2k)-th point of the Poisson process, so N(t) = ⌊P(t)/2⌋. Because ⌊n/2⌋ = (n − 1{n odd})/2, the formula for m(t) is correct.
P(P(t) odd) = e^(−λt) sinh(λt) = (1 − e^(−2λt))/2. This gives m(t) = λt/2 − 1/4 + e^(−2λt)/4. The difference m(t)/t − λ/2 = (e^(−2λt) − 1)/(4t) is correct.
3 · 100/2 − 1/4 = 149.75 = 599/4, and I recomputed this value. The term e^(−600)/4 is negligible. The constant −1/4 = E ξ²/(2µ²) − 1 = 3/4 − 1 is also correct.

nm:statphys-blackwell-renewal.why: Source claim: Dippon and Walk Theorem 1 states the limit for nonarithmetic nonnegative steps, with 1/EX₁ = 0 for infinite mean. Their introduction lists many proofs and monographs since Blackwell (1948). The record has no use evidence, so I judged the other scores from the mathematics. Inference: the key renewal theorem, limits of regenerative processes and the Cramér–Lundberg approximation rest on it, so res is 4. The nonarithmetic condition excludes lattice laws, so hyp is 3. The proof needs Arzelà–Ascoli, martingale convergence, Hewitt–Savage and closed subgroups of ℝ, so pro is 1.

review.conditions: The statement needs nonnegative i.i.d. steps with P(ξ₁ = 0) < 1 and a nonarithmetic law, and it allows µ = ∞. The limit h/µ for the 4 window types is correct. The atom of U at 0 does not change the limit.
review.prerequisites: Tonelli wd:Q7820874, Arzelà–Ascoli wd:Q1477053, dominated convergence wd:Q1067156, Doob wd:Q1765521, Hewitt–Savage and Fatou wd:Q5437947 cover the steps. Step s4 also uses the classification of closed subgroups of ℝ. This is an elementary fact, not an absent result.
review.alignment: Dippon and Walk p. 3 assume F(0) < 1 and a nonarithmetic law, and Theorem 1 on p. 4 states the limit. The alignment text is correct but incomplete. The source also proves the general case without moments, with a different 2nd step that reduces to the case EX₁³ < ∞. The Arzelà–Ascoli selection is in the 1st source step, not the 3rd.
review.why: All 6 proof steps are correct. The martingale proof of the Choquet–Deny step is complete, and the trapezoid sandwich gives all window types. The application values 1 and 0.99992 are correct. The alignment text needs a small correction, but this is not a reason to defer.

step_reviews.why: With ξ ≥ 0 the walk is nondecreasing, so {N_a > mK} = {T_(mK) ≤ a}, and the block bound gives V(a) < ∞. The walk after σ has the law of (T_j), so U(I) ≤ V(a). The renewal equation and the tail identity follow from independence and Tonelli.

The bounds on w follow from U(I) ≤ V(|I|). The supports of z(x − ·) and of a difference of 2 translates have length at most 2b + 1. Arzelà–Ascoli and a diagonal argument give g. Dominated convergence with bounded w gives g = F ∗ g.

M_n = g(x − T_n) is a bounded martingale, because g = F ∗ g and ξ_(n+1) is independent of F_n. Its limit is a symmetric function of the steps, so Hewitt–Savage makes it constant. Then M₁ = E[M_∞ | F₁] = g(x) almost surely.

Step s3 and continuity give g(y) = g(y + p) for all y and all p in the support S. The period group is closed and contains a positive point. If it were δℤ, F would be arithmetic. So it is ℝ and g is constant.

Tonelli and the tail identity give ∫₀^∞ w(x − t)(1 − F(t)) dt = ∫_(−∞)^x z. Along τ_k, w(τ_k − t) → κ for every t. Dominated convergence for µ < ∞ and Fatou for µ = ∞ give κ = (∫ z)/µ. The subsequence argument then gives the full limit.
The trapezoids satisfy z₋(t + h − y) ≤ 1_I(y) ≤ z₊(t + h − y) for each of the 4 window types. Their integrals are h − c and h + c. Step s5 and c → 0 give U(I) → h/µ.

computation_reviews.why: The gaps of a scale-of-two counter have the Gamma(2, 4) law, which is positive with a density and mean 1/2. So the hypotheses hold, and h/µ = (1/2)/(1/2) = 1.
T_n has the Gamma(2n, λ) density λ^(2n) t^(2n−1) e^(−λt)/(2n − 1)!. The sum over n ≥ 1 is λ e^(−λt) sinh(λt) = (λ/2)(1 − e^(−2λt)). The atom of U at 0 does not affect windows in (0, ∞).
The integral of (λ/2) e^(−2λs) over (t, t + h] is (e^(−2λt) − e^(−2λ(t+h)))/4. At λ = 4, t = 1 and h = 1/2 the value is 1 − 8.23 × 10^(−5) = 0.99992. I recomputed it with Python.
Gaps 1 or 2 have span 1 and mean 3/2, so Erdős–Feller–Pollard gives U({n}) → 2/3. The windows [n + 1/4, n + 3/4] contain no integer, so U is 0 there. Thus U([t, t + 1/2]) has no limit.

review.conditions: The statement allows a signed Borel h with absolutely summable upper and lower sums and a gap that goes to 0. It allows µ = ∞. The finiteness of H(t), the limit and the version on (0, t] are all correct.
review.prerequisites: Step s2 uses nm:statphys-blackwell-renewal for the windows J_k(t) = (t − (k + 1)δ, t − kδ], and the Blackwell record covers half-open windows. Step s1 proves the local bound U(I) ≤ C_δ again in place. No other result is necessary.
review.alignment: Gallager Theorem 4.7.3 on p. 202 states the theorem for r ≥ 0 and dm and says that it gives no proof. Durrett Theorem 2.6.12 on pp. 101-102 has the step function and Riemann sum proof. The alignment text describes both sources correctly.
review.why: All 4 proof steps are correct and follow Durrett's proof with more detail. The application checks direct Riemann integrability for a monotone h_x. The limits 9/16 and 20/3 minutes are correct.

step_reviews.why: The local bound repeats the block and shift argument of the Blackwell record. The point t − s is in cell k exactly when s is in J_k(t). Summable |M_k| + |m_k| makes H(t) finite and gives h(x) → 0. The 2 integrals differ by h(t)U({0}), and U({0}) is finite.
Blackwell's theorem applies to each window J_k(t), whose left end goes to ∞. By step s1 the tail k ≥ K is at most ε for all t. So the integral of the step function converges to (δ/µ) Σ a_k.

g₋ ≤ h ≤ g₊ on [0, ∞), and both step functions have summable coefficients by hypothesis. U ≥ 0 gives the sandwich for H(t), and step s2 gives the bounds I_δ/µ and Ī_δ/µ. So h is integrable, because |h| ≤ |g₊| + |g₋|.
The hypothesis Ī_δ − I_δ → 0 and I_δ ≤ ∫ h ≤ Ī_δ make both sums converge to ∫ h. So lim H(t) = (1/µ) ∫ h. For µ = ∞ both bounds are 0.

computation_reviews.why: B_t > x holds exactly when the last renewal T_n ≤ t has T_(n+1) > t + x. Only 1 index n satisfies T_n ≤ t < T_(n+1), so the events are disjoint. Independence of ξ_(n+1) and T_n gives the integral against U.
For a nonincreasing h_x, M_k = h_x(kδ) and m_k ≥ h_x((k + 1)δ). The gap sum telescopes to at most δ h_x(0) ≤ δ. Also δ Σ M_k ≤ δ + ∫ h_x is finite, so h_x is directly Riemann integrable.
The uniform law on [0, 20] has a density, so it is nonarithmetic, and µ = 10. The integral ∫_x^20 (1 − y/20) dy is (20 − x)²/40, so the limit is (20 − x)²/400. For x = 5 it is 225/400 = 9/16.
Tonelli gives E B_t = ∫ P(B_t > x) dx = ∫_[0,t] h(t − s) U(ds) with h(u) = E(ξ − u)⁺. This h is nonincreasing and integrable, so the argument of a2 applies. E ξ²/2 = 200/3 and E ξ²/(2µ) = 20/3.

review.why: All 4 proof steps are correct. The record adds the detail that limits pass along the integer valued N(t) → ∞. The age replacement values 15/4, 2, 8/15 and 1/15 are correct.

The only hypothesis is a standard Brownian motion, so hyp is 4.

review.conditions: The envelope ψ(t) = √(2t log log t) for t > e is correct. The statement has both the lim sup and the lim inf, with the almost sure quantifier. The definition of a standard linear Brownian motion is complete. The statement is true as written.
review.prerequisites: Part (b) of the reflection principle record gives P(max B ≥ a) = P(|B(t)| ≥ a) for s2. The first Borel–Cantelli lemma gives s2, and the second Borel–Cantelli lemma gives s4. The symmetry of Brownian motion in s5 and s6 is a basic property.
review.alignment: I confirmed Theorem 5.1 at the top of p. 119 and the lim inf in Remark 5.2 in the local copy. The source proof uses the same geometric sequence, the same events A_n and D_n, and Lemma 12.9 for the tails. The record proves the tail bounds in s1 and uses integer q in the lower bound, which is a harmless change.
review.why: Accept. All 6 proof steps are correct, and I checked each exponent and each ratio of ψ values. The application arithmetic 9/(2 · (3/4)²) = 8 is correct. Step a4 gives the rate of a valid boundary in an informal way. The claim is correct for boundaries of the form cψ(t).

step_reviews.why: The bound P(Z > x) ≤ φ(x)/x and the identity φ(x)/x = ∫(1 + u^{−2})φ du are correct. For x ≥ 1, x/(1 + x²) ≥ 1/(2x) and φ(x)/x ≤ e^{−x²/2}. The derivative log log t + 1/log t is positive for t > e, so ψ increases.

The reflection principle gives P(A_n) = 2P(Z ≥ x_n) with x_n = (1 + ε)√(2 log(n log q)). Step s1 gives P(A_n) ≤ 2(n log q)^{−(1+ε)²}, which is summable. The Borel–Cantelli lemma then applies. The step is correct.

For q^{n−1} ≤ t < q^n with n − 1 ≥ n₀, B(t) is at most the maximum up to q^n. Since ψ increases, ψ(t) ≥ ψ(q^{n−1}). The ratio ψ(q^n)/ψ(q^{n−1}) tends to √q. The countable choice ε = 1/k, q = 1 + 1/k gives the bound 1.

Increments over disjoint intervals are independent, so the events D_n are independent. The value φ(y_n) = 1/(√(2π) log(q^n − q^{n−1})) is correct. For n ≥ log q, y_n ≤ 2√(log n), so P(D_n) ≥ c/(n√(log n)). The series diverges, and the second Borel–Cantelli lemma applies.

Step s3 for −B gives −B(q^{n−1}) ≤ 2ψ(q^{n−1}) for large n. The bound ψ(q^{n−1})/ψ(q^n) ≤ 1/√q and the limit √(1 − 1/q) of ψ(q^n − q^{n−1})/ψ(q^n) are correct. The limit q → ∞ through integers uses countably many null sets.
Steps s3 and s5 together give lim sup = 1. The lim inf of B is minus the lim sup of −B, and −B is a standard Brownian motion. So lim inf = −1 almost surely. The step is correct.

computation_reviews.why: Since lim sup S(t)/ψ(t) = 1 almost surely, S(t) ≥ (3/4)ψ(t) holds at arbitrarily large times. The only hypothesis is that S is a standard Brownian motion under the null hypothesis. The step is correct.
At such times Z(t) ≥ (3/4)√(2 log log t). The condition (3/4)√(2 log log t) ≥ 3 is 2 log log t ≥ 16, that is log log t ≥ 8. I recomputed 9/(2 · (3/4)²) = 8.
The large times of a1 are unbounded, so one of them has log log t ≥ 8, and there Z(t) ≥ 3. The level 1 − Φ(3) ≈ 0.00135 is correct. The bound t ≥ e^{e^8} is correct.

The argument works for each threshold c because √(2 log log t) → ∞. The upper bound gives S(t) ≤ (1 + ε)ψ(t) for all large t. The last sentence is informal. It is correct for boundaries of the form cψ(t), but not for every irregular boundary.

nm:statphys-ito-formula.why: Source: the statement is the d-dimensional form of Theorem 5.10 in the Lyons notes, which follow Le Gall. The packet has no use evidence. Thus I judge influence and application from the mathematics. Itô's formula is the central rule of stochastic calculus in probability, physics and finance. The proof needs stochastic integrals, brackets and weak convergence of measures, so pro is 1.

review.conditions: The statement has continuous semimartingale components and F in C². It has the almost sure quantifier for all t ≥ 0 and the bracket term with the factor 1/2. The conclusion that F(X) is a continuous semimartingale is correct. The statement is true as written.
review.prerequisites: Taylor's theorem, the Itô isometry, dominated convergence, Heine–Cantor, Slutsky, polarization, Borel–Cantelli and Helly–Bray each give what the step uses. Steps s3 and s4 also use the convergence of sums of squared increments to the bracket, which is Le Gall Proposition 4.21. The record puts this fact in its definition of the bracket, and I accept that.
review.alignment: I confirmed Theorem 5.10 on p. 68, the d-dimensional form on p. 69, Proposition 5.9, Lemma 5A, Lemma 5B and the proof on pp. 69-70. The record uses the integral remainder in place of the intermediate point ξ_{n,i}. It proves the Riemann sum step with the isometry. The alignment field describes these changes honestly.
review.why: Accept. All 5 proof steps are correct. The argument with the stopping times T_p in s2 is complete. The subsequence argument in s4 is also complete. The application gives E|X_4|² = 12, E|X_4|⁴ = 240 and α₂ = 0. A check with the χ² law with 3 degrees of freedom gives the same values.

step_reviews.why: The remainder R(x, y) = ∫(1 − u)∇²F(x + u(y − x)) du is continuous, and R(x, x) = ∇²F(x)/2. The expansion F(y) − F(x) = ∇F(x)·(y − x) + (y − x)ᵀR(y − x) is correct. The sum over k of the increments of F(X) gives S¹ₙ + S²ₙ.

Before T_p, |H| ≤ p, so |Hⁿ − H| ≤ 2p, and uniform continuity gives uniform convergence to 0. The isometry for the bounded martingale M^{T_p} and dominated convergence give L² convergence. The finite variation part tends to 0 for each path. P(T_p < t) → 0 gives convergence in probability.

The segments between X_{t_k} and X_{t_{k+1}} lie in a closed ball, which is compact and convex. Uniform continuity of ∇²F on that ball gives εₙ → 0 almost surely. The bound |S²ₙ − Qₙ| ≤ εₙ Σ|ΔX_k|² and Slutsky give S²ₙ − Qₙ → 0 in probability.

Polarization writes each product of increments as a difference of 2 squares. Along a subsequence, the distribution functions of ν±ₙ converge on a dense set to continuous brackets. Helly–Bray then gives convergence of the integrals of ∂_i∂_jF(X). The subsequence criterion gives convergence in probability.

The identity F(X_t) − F(X₀) = S¹ₙ + (S²ₙ − Qₙ) + Qₙ holds for every n. Limits in probability are almost surely unique, so the formula holds for each t. Rational t and continuity of both sides give all t ≥ 0 at once.

computation_reviews.why: With F = |x|², the second order term is (1/2) · 2 · 2D · d · t = 2dDt. The stochastic integral has a square integrable integrand, so it is a martingale with mean 0. I recomputed 2 · 3 · (1/2) · 4 = 12.

∂_iF = 4|x|²x_i and ∂_i²F = 8x_i² + 4|x|², so the sum over i is 4(d + 2)|x|². The bracket 2Dt and the factor 1/2 give 4D(d + 2)∫|X_s|² ds. The martingale part has mean 0 because its integrand has finite moments.
E|X_t|⁴ = 4D(d + 2) · 2dD · t²/2 = 4D²d(d + 2)t². I recomputed 4 · (1/4) · 3 · 5 · 16 = 240. A direct check gives E|B_4|⁴ = 16 · 15 = 240 for a 3-dimensional Brownian motion.
The non-Gaussian parameter in d dimensions is d E|X|⁴/((d + 2)(E|X|²)²) − 1. I recomputed 3 · 240/(5 · 144) − 1 = 0. This agrees with the Gaussian law of free Brownian diffusion.

The proof needs Itô's formula and characteristic functions, so pro is 2.

review.conditions: The statement needs a continuous adapted process, continuous local martingale components and ⟨X^i, X^j⟩_t = δ_ij t. Condition (i) asks that X_t − X_s is independent of F_s with the law N(0, (t − s)I). X₀ is free, which agrees with the local martingale definition of the record. The statement is true as written.
review.prerequisites: Itô's formula gives the exponential local martingale in s2. Dominated convergence for conditional expectations gives the true martingale in s3. The uniqueness of a law with a given characteristic function gives s4, and the record links it to the Fourier inversion theorem.
review.alignment: I confirmed Theorem 5.12 on p. 72 and its proof on p. 73 in the local copy. The source applies Proposition 5.11 with λ = i to ξ·X, and the record applies Itô's formula directly to (X, t). The source refers to Chapter 4 for (i) ⇒ (ii), and the record writes it out. review.why: Accept. All 4 proof steps are correct. The cancellation of the ds terms in s2 and the division by Z_s in s3 are correct. The application uses bounded progressive integrands with bracket t, so W is a Brownian motion and E W_2⁴ = 12.

step_reviews.why: The increments of Y have mean 0 and covariance (t − s)I and are independent of F_s, so Y^i is a martingale. The expansion of Y^iY^j gives the conditional mean δ_ij(t − s). Thus Y^iY^j − δ_ij t is a martingale, and uniqueness of the bracket gives δ_ij t.

The process (X, t) has continuous semimartingale components, and t has zero bracket with all of them. The derivatives of F give the terms iξ_jZ, (|ξ|²/2)Z and −ξ_jξ_kZ. The 2 ds terms cancel because ⟨X^j, X^k⟩_t = δ_jk t. So Z is a complex continuous local martingale.

|Z_t| = e^{|ξ|²t/2} is bounded on [0, T]. The martingale property of the stopped process passes to the limit by conditional dominated convergence. Division by the F_s-measurable Z_s gives E[exp(iξ·(X_t − X_s)) | F_s] = exp(−|ξ|²(t − s)/2).

The bounded F_s-measurable factor exp(iη·W) gives the joint characteristic function of a product law. Uniqueness of the law gives independence of W and X_t − X_s and the Gaussian law. The choice W = 1_A for A in F_s gives independence from F_s.

computation_reviews.why: cos θ and sin θ are bounded and progressive, so W is a continuous L² martingale. The bracket is ∫(cos²θ + sin²θ) ds = t because ⟨B¹, B²⟩ = 0. Lévy's characterization with d = 1 applies, so W is an (F_t)-Brownian motion.
An (F_t)-Brownian motion with W₀ = 0 has W_t ~ N(0, t) and independent increments. The moments E W_t² = t and E W_t⁴ = 3t² of a centred Gaussian law are correct.
I recomputed 3 · 2² = 12 for t = 2. The value E W_2⁴ = 12 follows from step a2. The remark about the path dependence of θ is correct.
For a fixed angle with cos θ = 3/5 and sin θ = 4/5, the bracket is (9/25 + 16/25)t = t. I recomputed (3/5)² + (4/5)² = 1. The cross bracket ⟨B¹, W⟩_t = (3/5)t is correct.

nm:statphys-burkholder-davis-gundy.why: Source: the statement is Theorem 5.16 of the Lyons notes for p > 0, with explicit constants that I recomputed from the proof. The packet has no use evidence. Thus I judge influence and application from the mathematics. BDG is a standard tool for moment bounds of stochastic integrals and for SDE and SPDE estimates. The good-λ proof has several arguments with stopping times, so pro is 2.

review.conditions: The statement holds for all p > 0, all continuous local martingales with M₀ = 0 and all stopping times T. Both sides can be infinite. The constants C_p = 2^{p(p+1)/2 + p + 1} and c_p = 2^{−p²/4 − 2p − 1} follow from the choices of b in s4. The statement is true as written.
review.prerequisites: Martingale convergence and dominated convergence give s1. Doob's maximal inequality gives the second fact in s3, in its L² form, which follows from the weak form in the linked record. Fubini gives the tail formula in s4, and monotone convergence gives s5.
review.alignment: I confirmed Theorem 5.16, Proposition 5C, Corollaries 5D and 5E and the proof on pp. 77-79 in the local copy. The record follows the same good-λ route without Itô's formula. It replaces the reference to Proposition 4.12 with a short proof in s3. It adds the localization and the explicit constants, as the alignment field says.
review.why: Accept. All 5 proof steps are correct, and the constants agree with the choices b = 2^{−p−1} and b = 2^{−p/2−3}. The localization in s5 makes the subtraction of finite moments valid. The application gives 2⁸ · (1/4)⁴ = 1 and the Hölder bound 3/8 correctly.

step_reviews.why: The stopped process is a bounded martingale with mean 0, so its limit L has E L = 0. L = a on A, L ≥ −b off A and L = 0 when N* = 0. With A ⊂ {N* > 0}, this gives P(A) ≤ bP(N* > 0)/(a + b).

On the event, X − Y ≥ −sup Y > −β at all times. At some time X_t > α − (β − sup Y), so X − Y > α − β there. Thus X − Y hits α − β and never hits −β. Step s1 with a = α − β and b = β gives the factor β/α.

Both null set facts are correct, the second with Doob's L² inequality for N stopped when ⟨N⟩ reaches ε. In the upper case, N* ≥ M* − √r and ⟨N⟩ ≤ ⟨M⟩ give the inclusion. In the lower case, ⟨N⟩_∞ = (⟨M⟩_∞ − r)⁺ and N* ≤ 2M* give it.

The tail formula E X^q = κ^q ∫ q r^{q−1}P(X ≥ κr) dr is correct with κ = 4, b and 1. The finite moment condition makes the subtraction valid. I recomputed the constants: b = 2^{−p−1} gives 2^{p(p+1)/2 + p + 1}, and b = 2^{−p/2−3} gives 2^{p²/4 + 2p + 1}.

M^{T_n} is bounded by n and ⟨M^{S_n}⟩ is bounded by n, so the finite moment conditions of s4 hold. Monotone convergence removes the localization in both bounds. The identities (M^T)*_∞ = M*_T and ⟨M^T⟩_∞ = ⟨M⟩_T give a general stopping time T.

computation_reviews.why: N is a continuous local martingale for the shifted filtration, with N₀ = 0 and ⟨N⟩_u ≤ K²u. The deterministic time t − s is a stopping time. BDG gives E|M_t − M_s|^p ≤ C_pK^p|t − s|^{p/2}.
I recomputed 2⁸ · (1/4)⁴ = 256/256 = 1. So E|M_t − M_s|⁸ ≤ C_8 = 2^45 for these data. The step is correct.

With β = p/2 − 1 > 0 for p > 2, the bound has the form of the Kolmogorov hypothesis. Kolmogorov gives Hölder exponents γ < β/p on each bounded interval. M has continuous paths, so M itself has this regularity almost surely.
I recomputed (8/2 − 1)/8 = 3/8. As p → ∞, (p/2 − 1)/p → 1/2. So the paths are Hölder of every order below 1/2, as for Brownian motion.

nm:statphys-extremal-index.why: Source claim: Leadbetter and Rootzén (1987) prove θ ≤ 1 on p. 12. They state the level equivalence and Theorem 2.2.1 on p. 13. The record has no use evidence, so I judged influence and application from the mathematics. Inference: the extremal index is the standard measure of clusters of extremes in stationary series, so res is 4 and pra is 3. The proof needs only the union bound, the i.i.d. criterion and subsequences, so pro is 3.

review.conditions: The statement assumes strict stationarity and an extremal index θ with levels u_n(τ) for each τ > 0. It claims 0 ≤ θ ≤ 1 with no other condition. The power relation needs θ > 0, and the third hypothesis states this. The equivalence covers every ρ in [0, 1], also ρ = 0 and ρ = 1.
review.prerequisites: Steps s3, s4 and s5 use the i.i.d. criterion of nm:statphys-poisson-exceedance-criterion for 0 ≤ τ ≤ ∞. Its proof works along any subsequence of n, and step s5 needs this form. The union bound and the compactness of [0, ∞] are elementary. No result prerequisite is absent.
review.alignment: I read Leadbetter and Rootzén (1987) in the local copy. The union bound argument for θ ≤ 1 is on p. 12. The level equivalence is on p. 13, before Theorem 2.2.1, and the source attributes it to obvious arguments in [64]. The alignment field states these facts correctly.
review.why: All 6 proof steps are valid, and all 4 application steps are correct. The ARMAX example is stationary because exp(−a/x) exp(−(1 − a)/x) = exp(−1/x). I recomputed θ = 1/4, 92/365 ≈ 0.25205 and e^(−0.25205) ≈ 0.7772.

step_reviews.why: The union bound and stationarity give P(M_n > u_n(τ)) ≤ n(1 − F(u_n(τ))) → τ. Thus 1 − e^(−θτ) ≤ τ for every τ > 0, and the limit τ ↓ 0 gives θ ≤ 1. This matches the source on p. 12.

For v ≤ w the difference of the two events needs some ξ_i in (v, w]. The union bound gives 0 ≤ P(M_n ≤ w) − P(M_n ≤ v) ≤ n(F(w) − F(v)). Thus two level sequences with the same limit of n(1 − F) give the same limit.

The prerequisite gives F(v_n)^n → e^(−τ) if and only if n(1 − F(v_n)) → τ, for 0 ≤ τ ≤ ∞. Its proof uses only the values of the sequence, so the criterion also holds along subsequences. Lemma 1.2.2 of the source is this criterion.

The 3 cases are correct. For 0 < τ < ∞ step s2 gives the limit e^(−θτ). For τ = 0 the union bound gives the limit 1. For τ = ∞ the levels satisfy v_n < u_n(σ) for each σ and large n, so the limit is 0.

Every subsequence has a further subsequence with n(1 − F(v_n)) → τ′ in the compact set [0, ∞]. Step s4 gives the limit e^(−θτ′) = ρ^θ there. The map τ ↦ e^(−θτ) is injective for θ > 0, so τ′ = −log ρ and the full sequence converges.

The choice v_n = x/a_n + b_n and ρ = G(x) in steps s4 and s5 gives the equivalence at each x. The map t ↦ t^θ is a homeomorphism of [0, 1], so G and G^θ have the same continuity points. This is Theorem 2.2.1 of the source.

computation_reviews.why: The process is stationary because exp(−a/x) exp(−(1 − a)/x) = exp(−1/x). Then P(M_n ≤ u) = exp(−1/u) exp(−(n − 1)(1 − a)/u), and the limit at u_n(τ) is e^(−(1 − a)τ). Thus θ = 1 − 3/4 = 1/4.
The i.i.d. comparison has unit Fréchet maxima with G(x) = exp(−1/x) after division by n. The theorem gives the limit G(x)^(1/4) = exp(−1/(4x)) for the ARMAX maxima. The exact product formula agrees.
I recomputed (1 + 364/4)/365 = 92/365 ≈ 0.25205 and the limit value 91.25/365 = 0.25. The finite n value is close to the limit, so the comparison is correct.
I recomputed e^(−0.25205) ≈ 0.7772 and e^(−1) ≈ 0.368. The mean cluster size 1/θ = 4 is the standard meaning of the extremal index for this ARMAX process.

review.conditions: The hypotheses are those of the source. They are A ≥ 0, E A^κ = 1, E A^κ log⁺ A < ∞ and E|B|^κ < ∞. The law of log A given A > 0 is nonarithmetic. The record defines nonarithmetic as no lattice hℤ, as Kevei does on p. 2. The statement allows c₊ = 0. It claims c₊ > 0 only for B ≥ 0 with P(B > 0) > 0, and this claim is correct.
review.prerequisites: Hölder, Minkowski, Fubini and dominated convergence give what steps s1, s2, s4, s5 and s7 use. The linked nm:statphys-key-renewal covers only nonnegative steps, but step s5 needs the whole-line form. The reason text now says this honestly and cites Feller Vol. II, Section XI.9. The catalog has no record for the whole-line form. For an outline proof, the published citation supplies the step.
review.alignment: I read Kevei, arXiv:1609.07339, pp. 1-3, and arXiv:1512.07262, pp. 6-11. Steps s3 to s5 match equations (17) to (23). review.why: All 7 proof steps and all 4 application steps are correct. I checked the equality case of Hölder, the tilted mean, the bound (1 + e/(e − 1)) ∫|ψ| and the removal of the smoothing. Small doubt: the catalog has no whole-line key renewal record, so step s5 rests on the Feller citation. This is not a reason to defer.

step_reviews.why: Hölder with exponents κ/s and κ/(κ − s) gives the bound. Equality needs P(A > 0) = 1 and a constant A, thus A = 1, which is arithmetic. Subadditivity for s ≤ 1 and Minkowski for s > 1 give E|X|^s < ∞. The iteration argument gives uniqueness in law.

The tilted law is equivalent to the law of log A given A > 0, so it has the same lattice property. The bound a^κ|log a| ≤ 1/(eκ) is correct. Convexity of h with h(s) < 1 = h(κ) makes the left derivative positive. Dominated convergence identifies it with μ.

On {A > 0}, independence gives P(AX > e^x | A) = P(X > e^(x − log A)). Also e^(κx) = A^κ e^(κ(x − log A)). Thus e^(κx) P(AX > e^x) = E_κ f(x − log A). This gives f = ψ + f ∗ F_κ, as in equations (17) to (19) of Kevei.

The substitution t = e^x and X =d AX + B give the integral. Fubini gives κ⁻¹ E|((AX + B)₊)^κ − ((AX)₊)^κ|. The mean value bound with c_κ = max(1, 2^(κ−2)) is correct. Hölder with exponents κ and κ/(κ − 1) and step s1 make the bound finite.

I checked the remainder formula with the substitution y = x + log(A₁⋯A_n). It tends to 0 by step s1 and dominated convergence. The bound over unit intervals with the constant 1 + e/(e − 1) is correct, so ψ̂ is directly Riemann integrable. Feller Vol. II, Section XI.9 gives the whole-line key renewal theorem.

The substitution gives G(u) = u f̂(log u). Monotonicity of P(X > t) bounds G(bu) − G(u) from above and below. I checked both limit bounds. Both tend to c₊ as b decreases to 1, because (b − 1)/(b^(κ+1) − 1) tends to 1/(κ + 1).

The formula for c₊ follows from ∫ψ with the substitution t = e^x. The pair (−X, −B) satisfies the same hypotheses. For B ≥ 0, Fubini gives ∫ t^(κ−1) 1{AX ≤ t < AX + B} dt = κ⁻¹((AX + B)^κ − (AX)^κ). This expectation is positive when P(B > 0) > 0.

computation_reviews.why: For log A ∼ N(−1/2, 1), E A^κ = exp(−κ/2 + κ²/2). The exponent is 0 at κ = 1, the only positive root. The other hypotheses hold, because log A is normal and B ≡ 1.
Under P_κ the density of log A gets the factor e^(κx). This shifts the normal mean by κσ² = 1, from −1/2 to 1/2. Thus μ = 1/2, which is in (0, ∞).
With B ≡ 1 and κ = 1, (AX + 1) − AX = 1 at every point. Thus c₊ = 1/(1 · 1/2) = 2, and I recomputed this value. The positivity part applies because B > 0.
The value 2/1000 = 0.002 is correct as a first-order value. The tail index 1 gives E X = ∞. The series Σ (E A)^n with E A = e^0 = 1 also diverges, so the two facts agree.

The block of σ(n) in Π is the image of the block of n in Π′. The bijection π is a function of (Π, σ), so U′ is again i.i.d. uniform and independent of Π′. Thus (X_(σ(n))) has the law of (X_n).
De Finetti's theorem applies to the exchangeable sequence (X_n) in [0, 1] and gives F. Glivenko–Cantelli, applied conditionally on F, gives (2.12) of the source. Both prerequisites are in the record.

Conditionally on F, 2 draws coincide almost surely only at a common atom. A quantile map sends J_k to the k-th atom and the rest of [0, 1] to the continuous part. This gives the paintbox law, which depends only on the atom sizes.

The jumps of F_n are the block sizes of Π_n divided by n. Each jump differs from the jump of F by at most 2 sup |F_n − F|, and the decreasing rearrangement is 1-Lipschitz. Thus N↓_(n,i)/n → P↓_i, and the tower property gives the law given P↓.

computation_reviews.why: In the paintbox, P(1 ∼ 2 | p) = Σ p_k², so P(1 ∼ 2) = E[Σ (P↓_k)²]. The process gives 1/(1 + θ) = 1/2 for θ = 1. The hypotheses hold because the EPPF depends only on block sizes.
In the paintbox, P(1 ∼ 2 ∼ 3 | p) = Σ p_k³. The process gives (1/2)(2/3) = 1/3 for θ = 1. This agrees with the expected value.
Gene m + 1 does not join the singleton class of gene 1 with probability (m − 1 + θ)/(m + θ). For θ = 1 the product over m = 1, …, 9 is 1/10. The general product 1/n tends to 0.

Gene 1 is a singleton of Π exactly when U_1 is outside all intervals, almost surely. The events {1 alone in Π_n} decrease to this event, so its probability is lim 1/n = 0. Since 1 − Σ P↓_k ≥ 0 has mean 0, the frequencies are proper.

review.conditions: The statement needs Borel σ and b that are Lipschitz in x with one constant K. It also bounds σ(t, 0) and b(t, 0) on each [0, T]. These bounds give linear growth, so the integrals exist for continuous adapted X. Pathwise uniqueness allows a random X₀ with X₀ = X₀′ a.s., and the stop at |X| ≥ M handles it.
review.prerequisites: nm:doob-s-maximal-inequality gives the L² bound E sup|M|² ≤ 4E|M_t|² in steps s1 and s3, but its catalog form is the discrete weak-type inequality. nm:statphys-ito-isometry, nl:16121 and nl:18093 give what steps s1, s5 and s6 use. nm:gronwall-lemma is the differential form in mathlib, but step s2 uses the integral form of Lyons Lemma 8.4. review.why: All 6 proof steps are valid, and all 4 application steps are correct. The proof follows Lyons and adds the case τ = 0 and the L² convergence that the source gives only briefly. step_reviews.why: The inequality (a + b + c)² ≤ 3(a² + b² + c²) gives the factor 3. Doob's L² inequality and the isometry give 4K² ∫ E|X_{r∧τ} − Y_{r∧τ}|² dr, because X_r = X_{r∧τ} for r ≤ τ. Cauchy–Schwarz gives the factor t for the drift. The total is 3(4 + t)K², as in Lemma 8A.

On {τ > 0} both stopped paths stay in the closed ball of radius M, so g ≤ 4M² and g is finite. Step s1 with equal initial values gives g ≤ 3(4 + T)K² ∫ g. The integral Grönwall lemma gives g = 0. Then τ → ∞ as M → ∞ gives indistinguishability.

Each iterate is continuous and adapted to the completed filtration of B by induction. The integrands of X¹ − x are deterministic and bounded by A_T. Doob and Cauchy–Schwarz give g₁(t) ≤ 2·4tA_T² + 2t²A_T² = (8t + 2t²)A_T², which is correct.

Step s1 with τ = ∞ and equal initial values gives g_(n+1)(t) ≤ C_T ∫₀ᵗ g_n(r) dr. Induction from g₁ ≤ C′_T gives the factorial bound. I checked that the integral of r^(n−1)/(n − 1)! from 0 to t is t^n/n!.

The square roots of C^n T^n/n! have a finite sum. Cauchy–Schwarz gives E sup|X^(n+1) − Xⁿ| ≤ g_(n+1)(T)^(1/2), so the series of sup norms is finite a.s. Thus Xⁿ converges uniformly on [0, T]. Minkowski's inequality for the tail series gives L² convergence and a finite E sup|X|².

The Lipschitz bound and Cauchy–Schwarz give L² convergence of the drift integrals. The Itô isometry gives L² convergence of the stochastic integrals, because E|Xⁿ_s − X_s|² → 0 uniformly on [0, T]. The 2 limits agree a.s. for each t, and continuity in t gives the equation for all t.

computation_reviews.why: The product rule with the deterministic factor e^(−γt) gives dV = −γV dt + √(2γθ) dB. The drift −γv is Lipschitz with K = γ and σ is constant, so the uniqueness part applies to the candidate.
The integral of a deterministic integrand against B is Gaussian. The isometry gives 2γθ ∫₀ᵗ e^(−2γ(t−s)) ds = θ(1 − e^(−2γt)). The mean is e^(−γt)v.
At t = (ln 2)/γ, e^(−γt) = 1/2 and e^(−2γt) = 1/4. The mean is 2/2 = 1 m/s and the variance is 3/4 m²/s². Thus E V_t² = 1 + 3/4 = 7/4 m²/s², and the expression gives 1.75.
E V_t² = v²e^(−2γt) + θ(1 − e^(−2γt)) tends to θ = k_B T_f/m. Thus (1/2)m E V_t² tends to (1/2)k_B T_f, the equipartition value. The step is correct.

step_reviews.why: Uniqueness for the modified bounded problem gives agreement on F_(τ_ℓ). Continuous paths give τ_ℓ → ∞, so all solutions agree. This is the first reduction in the proof of Theorem 14.3.
The growth bounds give tr a + 2⟨b, x⟩ ≤ C′(1 + |x|²). Optional stopping gives E[e^(−C′τ_ℓ)] ≤ (1 + |x₀|²)/(1 + ℓ²). The limit of the P^ℓ agrees with the source on p. 4.
Under P the quadratic variation of x is ∫a ds, so the Girsanov exponent has the term ½∫⟨b, a⁻¹b⟩ds. Novikov holds for bounded a⁻¹b. This is item 2 of Chapter 10.
This is Lemma 14.1 of the source. The exit time argument and the use of regular conditional distributions after τ are correct. The final bound with P₁[τ_n ≤ t] + P₂[τ_n ≤ t] is correct.
I checked the sign. With u = −Gg, u_s + ½Δu = g, so the equation becomes g − ½∑[a_ij − δ_ij](Gg)_ij = f. The Jones bound makes this operator a contraction for small δ.
Itô's formula and u(T, ·) = 0 give E∫f dt = −u(s₀, x₀) with the correct sign. Theorem 11.2 states the estimate for d = 1 and L². Chapter 14 says that the rest is as in that case.

computation_reviews.why: With a ≡ 1 and b = −sgn x, L u = 1 − 2|x| ≤ u, so C′ = 1. The bound gives (1 + 0)/(1 + 9) = 1/10. Python agrees.

The drift is bounded, so Girsanov gives a law equivalent to Wiener measure on F_t. Thus P_0[x(t) = 0] = 0, and symmetry gives P_0[x(t) > 0] = 1/2.

These conditions make Lφ and (∇φ)ᵀg bounded. The stopping time must be for a filtration in which W is a Brownian motion and X is adapted, and the record meets this.

review.why: All 4 proof steps are valid, and all 4 application steps are correct. The proof is short and complete. The application uses the cut-off φ = uχ, then monotone convergence to show E τ < ∞ before it applies the formula at τ. This order is correct.

step_reviews.why: With dXⁱ = fᵢ dt + ∑ₖ gᵢₖ dWᵏ, the bracket is d⟨Xⁱ, Xʲ⟩ = (ggᵀ)ᵢⱼ dt. Itô's formula then gives the drift ∫ Lφ ds and the martingale part ∫ (∇φ)ᵀg dW. X is a continuous semimartingale because f and g are bounded on compact sets.
φ and its derivatives vanish outside the compact support K. On K, f and g are bounded, and the derivatives of φ are continuous and thus bounded. So 1 constant C bounds Lφ, h and φ on ℝⁿ.

h(X_s) is progressive and bounded by C, so E M_t² ≤ C²t and M is a square-integrable martingale on each [0, t]. Optional stopping at the bounded time τ ∧ N gives E M_(τ∧N) = 0. The expectation of step s1 at τ ∧ N gives the stopped formula.
E τ < ∞ gives τ < ∞ a.s., so τ ∧ N = τ for large N. Also |φ| ≤ C and |∫₀^(τ∧N) Lφ ds| ≤ Cτ, which is integrable. Dominated convergence on both sides gives the formula at τ.

computation_reviews.why: u″ = −1/D, so Lφ = D u″ = −1 on [0, ℓ], because χ = 1 there. For s < τ ∧ N, X_s is in (0, ℓ). The formula gives E φ(X_(τ∧N)) = φ(x) − E(τ ∧ N), and φ ≥ 0 on [0, ℓ] gives the bound.
Monotone convergence gives E τ ≤ φ(x) < ∞, so the theorem applies at τ. Then X_τ is 0 or ℓ, and u is 0 there. Thus E τ = φ(x) = x(ℓ − x)/(2D).
x(ℓ − x)/(2D) = 2 · 8/2 = 8. The unit is µm²/(µm²/s) = s. The expression gives 8.0.
x(ℓ − x) has its maximum ℓ²/4 at x = ℓ/2. Then E τ = ℓ²/(8D) = 100/8 = 12.5 s. The expression gives 12.5, which is 25/2.

review.conditions: The statement asks for a standard Brownian motion from 0, the occupation density local time and τ = inf{t : B_t = −1}. It gives the Markov property and the kernels on [−1, 0] and on [0, ∞).
review.prerequisites: Itô's excursion theorem gives the Poisson structure and n(sup f > δ) = 1/(2δ). The occupation times record gives the continuity of L in x. Dynkin gives the uniqueness of the law.
review.alignment: I checked Theorem 4 and its proof on p. 315 of Rogers. The source proves only the case (−1, 0) and says that x > 0 is similar. The alignment states this, and s5 writes out that case.
review.why: All 6 outline steps and all 4 application steps are correct. The Poisson sums give the BESQ(2) and BESQ(0) kernels exactly. The variance 12 agrees with the second derivative of (1 + 2λ)/(1 + 4λ) at 0.

step_reviews.why: The strong Markov property at H_a and Itô's excursion theorem at the level a give independent Poisson processes Ξ₊ and Ξ₋. Proposition 2 of the source gives n(sup f > δ) = 1/(2δ).
τ is in the first excursion below a that reaches the depth 1 + a. Its label is exponential with rate 1/(2(1 + a)), so the mean 2(1 + a) is correct. The split of the local times is correct.
Given Ξ₋, the points of Ξ₊ with label below ℓ form a Poisson process with a law that depends only on ℓ. This gives the conditional independence on p. 315 of the source.
K has the Poisson law with mean ℓ/(2δ), and each amount is exponential with mean 2δ. The sum gives (1 + 2δλ)^(−1) exp(−λℓ/(1 + 2δλ)), the BESQ(2) kernel for the time δ.
For a ≥ 0 the first piece stays below a and adds nothing above a. On {τ < H_a} the local times above a are 0, and ℓ = 0 gives the same kernel. The BESQ(0) kernel is correct.

L(τ, −1) = 0, and Laplace transforms determine laws on [0, ∞). The planar Gaussian computation gives the dimension 2 kernel. The case a = −1 of the statement needs continuity of Z at −1, which s6 does not say.

computation_reviews.why: Z_0 has the law of |W(1)|², exponential with mean 2. A direct check agrees: L(τ, 0) is exponential with rate n(inf f < −1) = 1/2.
With µ = λ/(1 + 2λ), 1/(1 + 2µ) = (1 + 2λ)/(1 + 4λ). I checked the algebra and the BESQ(0) kernel at the distance 1.
As λ → ∞, (1 + 2λ)/(1 + 4λ) → 1/2. The event Z_1 = 0 is the event that B hits −1 before 1, with probability 1/2.
The kernel gives mean z and variance 4z, so E Z_1² = 8 + 8 = 16 and the variance is 12. The second derivative of (1 + 2λ)/(1 + 4λ) at 0 is also 16.

It states the Poisson property for disjoint sets, with infinite counts for infinite means. It adds n(U) = ∞ and the value 1/(2a), which hold with this normalization.

review.why: All 6 proof steps are valid, and all 4 application steps are correct. The outline names the real ingredients in the order of Rogers and Itô. Step s4 rests on the classical result on jump counts of additive processes, and the scope says so. The application numbers agree with the gambler's ruin probability.

step_reviews.why: Tanaka's formula gives L continuous, nondecreasing and carried by Z. The source states on p. 310 that the growth set of L is Z. Thus γ_ℓ is a stopping time with B(γ_ℓ) = 0, and the jumps of γ are the excursion intervals.

The strong Markov property at γ_ℓ gives a Brownian motion from 0 that is independent of F(γ_ℓ). The excursions with labels at most ℓ end by γ_ℓ, so they are F(γ_ℓ)-measurable. The shifted point process is the excursion process of the new motion, as on p. 313.

At most mγ_t excursion intervals in [0, γ_t] are longer than 1/m, so the counts on U_m are finite. N has unit jumps, because 1 label carries 1 excursion. Stationary independent increments from s2 then make N a Poisson process.

The increments of Z* after t depend only on the shifted point process, so they are independent of F(γ_t). Z* jumps only with the Poisson process on U_m, so it is continuous in probability. This is the proof of Itô Theorem 3.1, and the limits keep the Poisson law and independence.

M is a measure by monotone convergence and does not change under shifts in local time by s2. M((0, t] × U_m) is finite, so M = Leb ⊗ n with σ-finite n, as in Itô Section 4. Infinitely many excursions occur before γ₁ > 0, so n(U) = ∞.

L_H is the label of the first excursion in A, so P(L_H > ℓ) = exp(−ℓ n(A)) and E L_H = 1/n(A). Optional sampling at H ∧ t and the 2 limit theorems give E L_H = a. Symmetry splits n(A) = 1/a into 2 equal parts.

computation_reviews.why: With a = 1/2 and b = 2, n(A) = 1/(2 · 1/2) = 1 and n(C) = 1/(2 · 2) = 1/4. The trap catches the molecule in the first excursion below −2, which is the first point in C.

A and C are disjoint, so their label processes are independent Poisson processes with rates 1 and 1/4. The local time before the trap is the first label in C, exponential with mean 4. Tanaka for B⁻ gives ½ E L = 2, the same mean.

For 2 independent Poisson processes, each next point is in A with probability 1/(1 + 1/4) = 4/5, independently. Thus P(M ≥ k) = (4/5)^k. For k = 1 this is b/(a + b) = 2/2.5 = 4/5, the gambler's ruin value.
E M = Σ_(k≥1) (4/5)^k = (4/5)/(1/5) = 4. The ratio n(A)/n(C) = 1/(1/4) = 4 agrees. The expression gives 4.0.

review.why: Accept. Every proof step and every application step is correct. I checked the identity (2 − √α)√α = 1 − (1 − √α)². I also checked u√α(1 − √α)/(1 − uα) = ½ and (1 − α)c = √α(1 − √α). The Novikov bound 4/3 for γ² = 3/4 is correct.

step_reviews.why: Itô's formula gives E(L) = 1 + ∫E(L) dL, so E(L) is a nonnegative local martingale. Conditional Fatou along τ_n gives the supermartingale property. If E Z_T = E Z₀, then Z_s − E[Z_t | F_s] is nonnegative with mean 0, so Z is a martingale.
The identity exp(½M_σ) = E(M)_σ^(1/2) exp(¼⟨M⟩_σ) holds pathwise. Cauchy–Schwarz and E E(M)_σ ≤ 1 from s1 give E exp(½M_σ) ≤ K^(1/2). The bound ⟨M⟩_σ ≤ ⟨M⟩_T holds because σ ≤ T.
A family bounded in L^u with u > 1 is uniformly integrable. Z_{T∧τ_n} → Z_T almost surely because τ_n → ∞. Vitali then gives E Z_T = E Z₀, and s1 gives the martingale property.

The identity E(√αM) = E(M)^α exp(√α(1 − √α)M) is correct. With u = 1/((2 − √α)√α), uα = √α/(2 − √α) < 1 and u√α(1 − √α)/(1 − uα) = ½. Hölder, s1 and s2 give the L^u bound K^((1 − uα)/2), so s3 applies.
Hölder with exponents 1/α and 1/(1 − α) gives the bound with c = √α/(1 + √α) < ½. Jensen and s2 give E exp(cM_T) ≤ K^c. The exponent (1 − α)c = √α(1 − √α) tends to 0 as α ↑ 1, so E E(M)_T ≥ 1.

computation_reviews.why: Jensen for the probability measure ds on [0, 1] and the convex function exp give the first bound. For γ²s < 1, E exp((γ²/2)B_s²) = (1 − γ²s)^(−1/2) is the correct Gaussian integral. Here γ² = 3/4, so γ²s < 1 on [0, 1].
Tonelli lets E pass inside ∫ ds. The integral ∫₀^1 (1 − γ²s)^(−1/2) ds equals 2(1 − √(1 − γ²))/γ². For γ² = 3/4 this is 2 · (1/2)/(3/4) = 4/3, which I confirmed.
The hypotheses hold with T = 1, M₀ = 0 and E exp(½⟨M⟩_1) ≤ 4/3 < ∞. Thus the criterion gives E E(M)_1 = 1. Since E(M)_1 > 0, Q is a probability measure equivalent to P.

step_reviews.why: All φ terms cancel in d_φ(x, y) − d_φ(x, z) − d_φ(z, y), and the remainder is ⟨∇φ(z) − ∇φ(y), x − z⟩. With z = x*, the sign of this term decides the Pythagorean inequality. The chord argument with strict convexity gives d_φ(u, v) > 0 for u ≠ v.

The point x_t lies in C ⊆ U, and φ is differentiable at x*. The chain rule gives g′(0+) = ⟨∇φ(x*) − ∇φ(y), x − x*⟩. Minimality makes all difference quotients nonnegative, so g′(0+) ≥ 0. Step s1 turns this into the Pythagorean inequality.
Step s2 with x* = x₁ and x = x₂ gives d_φ(x₂, y) ≥ d_φ(x₂, x₁) + d_φ(x₁, y). The 2 minimal values are equal and finite, so d_φ(x₂, x₁) ≤ 0. Step s1 then gives x₂ = x₁.
The hypothesis and the identity of step s1 give d_φ(x, y) ≥ d_φ(x, x*) + d_φ(x*, y). Since d_φ(x, x*) ≥ 0, d_φ(x, y) ≥ d_φ(x*, y) for all x ∈ C. Thus x* is a minimizer.

The line through x* and x lies in L. U is open, so x_t ∈ U ∩ L = C for small |t|. Thus g has an interior minimum at t = 0, and Fermat's theorem gives g′(0) = 0. The identity of step s1 then gives equality.

computation_reviews.why: (1 − 1/2)/2 = 1/4. The candidate (1/2, 1/4, 1/4) has positive entries, sum 1 and x₁ = 1/2, so it lies in C. C is convex and y lies in U, so the hypotheses hold.

∇φ(x) = (log x₁, log x₂, log x₃). log(1/3) − log(1/2) = log(2/3), and log(1/3) − log(1/4) = log(4/3). With x₂ + x₃ − 1/2 = 1/2 − x₁, the inner product is −(x₁ − 1/2) log 2 ≤ 0 on C. I checked it at 5 random points of C.
The converse part applies, so x* is the minimizer. (1/2) log(3/2) + 2 · (1/4) log(3/4) = (1/2) log(9/8). I computed 0.058892, which agrees with ≈ 0.0589.
x = (3/4, 1/8, 1/8) lies in C. The gap is −⟨∇φ(y) − ∇φ(x*), x − x*⟩ = (x₁ − 1/2) log 2 = (1/4) log 2. A direct computation of the 3 divergences gives 0.17329, which agrees with ≈ 0.173.
