review.conditions: The statement is true as written. The finite infimum D* is necessary for the differences of divergences in parts (a) and (b). Part (a) is trivial when D(Q‖P) = ∞. Part (c) needs closedness in total variation, and convexity of E keeps midpoints in E. The claim Q ≪ Q* follows from D(Q‖Q*) < ∞.
review.prerequisites: Step s1 uses Radon–Nikodym densities and Gibbs' inequality. Step s2 uses monotone convergence for q₁ − q_{1/k}. review.why: Accept. All 6 proof steps are valid, and all 4 application steps are correct. Step s2 treats the set {f* = 0 < f} correctly. There q₀ = −∞, so the bound ∫ q₀ dP ≥ 0 makes the set null. The worked case uses bits, and a change of units does not change the inequality.

step_reviews.why: φ(t) = t log t has its minimum −1/e at t = 1/e, so ∫ φ(f) dP is defined. The density of a mixture is the mixture of the densities. Pointwise convexity of φ then gives convexity of D(·‖P) and finiteness on segments.

Chord slopes of a convex function from a fixed end point do not decrease, so q_{1/k} decreases to the right derivative q₀. The 3 cases of q₀ are correct. Monotone convergence for q₁ − q_{1/k} ≥ 0 gives ∫ q_{1/k} dP → ∫ q₀ dP in [−∞, ∞). The limit is ≥ 0, so q₀ is integrable and P(f* = 0 < f) = 0.

f = 0 almost everywhere on {f* = 0}, so Q ≪ Q*. On {f* > 0}, (f − f*) log f* = q₀ − (f − f*) is integrable with integral ∫ q₀ dP ≥ 0. Thus ∫ f log f* dP ≥ D(Q*‖P). The split of D(Q‖Q*) into 2 integrable parts gives part (a).

Gibbs' inequality D(Q‖Q*) ≥ 0 and the inequality of (a) give D(Q‖P) ≥ D(Q*‖P) on E. For 2 minimizers, (a) gives D* ≥ D(Q₂‖Q₁) + D*, and D* < ∞ gives D(Q₂‖Q₁) = 0. Pinsker's inequality then gives Q₂ = Q₁.

Since f_i/m ≤ 2, the positive part of f_i log(f_i/m) is at most f_i log 2. The negative part is at most m/e. So D(Q_i‖M) is finite. The relation f₁ log m + f₂ log m = 2φ(m) and integration give the identity with all terms finite.

Midpoints lie in E, so D(M‖P) ≥ D*, and step s5 sends D(Q_m‖M) + D(Q_n‖M) to 0. Pinsker's inequality gives the Cauchy property in total variation. A fast subsequence, monotone convergence and Fatou's lemma give a limit density f in L¹. Closedness gives Q* ∈ E, and Fatou's lemma for φ + 1/e ≥ 0 gives D(Q*‖P) ≤ D*.

computation_reviews.why: (0 · 4 + 1 · 2 + 2 · 1)/7 = 4/7. The constraint E_Q[H] ≤ 4/7 holds with equality, so Q* ∈ E and the constraint is active.

log₂(Q*(k)/P(k)) = log₂(3 · 2^(−k)/Z) = log₂(3/Z) − k. Q* has full support, so the decomposition holds for every Q. log₂(12/7) − 4/7 = 0.20618. The gap 4/7 − E_Q[H] is ≥ 0 on E, so part (b) applies. Bits only rescale all divergences by 1/ln 2.
Q = (5/7, 1/7, 1/7) has E_Q[H] = 3/7 ≤ 4/7, so Q ∈ E. The gap is 4/7 − 3/7 = 1/7. A direct computation of the 3 divergences in bits gives 0.142857.

review.why: All 6 proof steps are valid, and all 4 application steps are correct. The proof is the Brascamp-Lieb route: 1-dimensional Brunn-Minkowski, level sets, truncation, induction and a Borel reduction. The worked example is Prékopa's theorem. step_reviews.why: The shift puts K′ in (−∞, 0] and L′ in [0, ∞), with 0 in both sets. So (1 − λ)K′ and λL′ lie in the sum and meet at most in {0}. The sum for K and L is a translate, so the bound holds.

Lebesgue measure on ℝ is inner regular on Borel sets, also with infinite measure. The suprema over K and L are independent, so they give (1 − λ)|A| + λ|B|. The Borel set C removes the problem that the sumset can be non-measurable.

The scale change keeps the hypothesis and multiplies both sides by a^(1−λ) b^λ. For 0 < t < 1 the level sets are nonempty Borel sets, and the hypothesis gives the sumset inclusion. The layer-cake formula and the weighted AM-GM bound finish the step. The AM-GM cases with 0 or ∞ are direct.

If ∫F = 0 or ∫G = 0, the convention 0 · ∞ = 0 makes the right side 0. The truncations are bounded, have a positive supremum for large M and keep the hypothesis. Monotone convergence along integer M gives the limit in [0, ∞].

The sections satisfy the hypothesis in ℝ^(n−1), because (1 − λ)(s₀, z₀) + λ(s₁, z₁) = (s, (1 − λ)z₀ + λz₁). Tonelli's theorem gives Borel slice integrals and the iterated integrals. Then step s4 applies to F, G and H.

The step sets f′ and g′ to 0 and h″ to ∞ on a Borel null set. Then f′ ≤ f, g′ ≤ g and h″ ≥ h everywhere, so the hypothesis holds for (f′, g′, h″). The integrals do not change, because the functions agree almost everywhere.

computation_reviews.why: Z(x) is positive and finite by the inputs, so −log reverses the inequality correctly. Convexity of V gives the hypothesis of the theorem in ℝ^k for f, g and h. The result is the convexity of W, which is Prékopa's theorem.

The Hessian [[1, −1], [−1, 2]] has determinant 1 and trace 3, so V is convex. I checked (y − x)²/2 + y²/2 = (y − x/2)² + x²/4. The Gaussian integral gives Z(x) = √π e^(−x²/4), and a numerical integral at x = 1.3 agreed.
(1/2)(0²/4) + (1/2)(2²/4) = 0 + 1/2 = 1/2. I recomputed this value with exact fractions. The inputs x₀ = 0, x₁ = 2 and λ = 1/2 are valid.
The midpoint is x = 1, and 1²/4 = 1/4 ≤ 1/2. The weights 1/2 and 1/2 add up to 1, so the constant −log √π cancels. The check agrees with convexity.

review.conditions: The statement needs a finite E and independent variables with the law µ. The upper bound holds for every set A, not only for closed sets, because L_N takes finitely many values. The total variation metric gives the Euclidean topology on the simplex, so the interior and the closure are the usual ones.
review.prerequisites: Step s3 uses the multinomial theorem for the sum of the type probabilities. Step s7 uses Gibbs' inequality for H ≥ 0 and the Heine-Borel theorem for the compactness of M₁(E). The bound m!/n! ≥ n^(m−n) and the continuity of t log t are elementary and need no catalog record.

review.why: All 7 proof steps are valid, and all 5 application steps are correct. Step s3 gives the lower bound for |T_N(ν)| by a correct factorial comparison. The worked example gives the rate (10/7) log 2 − log(7/3) ≈ 0.1429. I checked it with exact fractions and a grid search on the simplex.

step_reviews.why: Each value L_N(x) lies in {0, 1/N, …, 1} for each of the |E| points, so |𝓛_N| ≤ (N + 1)^|E|. The size of a type class is the multinomial coefficient. The step is correct.
Independence gives the product Π_y µ(y)^(Nν(y)). If the support of ν is in the support of µ, Σ_y ν(y) log µ(y) = −H(ν) − H(ν|µ). The zero case agrees with e^(−∞) = 0.

The upper bound follows from P_ν(L_N = ν) ≤ 1. The ratio formula is correct, and m!/n! ≥ n^(m−n) holds for m ≥ 0 and n ≥ 1. The product is N^(N(Σν′ − Σν)) = 1, because ν′ has support in the support of ν. The multinomial theorem makes all type probabilities add up to 1.
Step s2 with the two bounds of step s3 gives (N + 1)^(−|E|) e^(−N H(ν|µ)) ≤ P(L_N = ν) ≤ e^(−N H(ν|µ)). If H(ν|µ) = +∞, all 3 terms are 0. The step is correct.

The event {L_N ∈ A} is a finite disjoint union over A ∩ 𝓛_N. Each term is at most e^(−N inf_A H), and there are at most (N + 1)^|E| terms. Since N⁻¹ log(N + 1) → 0, the limsup bound holds for every set A.

The rounded measure ν_N is a type with support in S, and each coordinate differs from ν by at most |E|/N. Since ν_N(y_k) ≥ ν(y_k) > 0, ν_N is a probability measure. It lies in A° for large N, and H(ν_N|µ) → H(ν|µ) by continuity on the support of µ.

Gibbs' inequality gives H ≥ 0. H is +∞ off the closed convex set D and is continuous and convex on D, so H is convex with closed level sets. The simplex is compact by Heine-Borel, so the level sets are compact. Steps s5 and s6 then give the principle.

computation_reviews.why: µ has full support, so H(·|µ) is finite and continuous on M₁(E). The map m is linear and 10/7 lies in (0, 2), so A° = {m > 10/7} and its closure is A. Thus the two bounds agree and the limit exists.
Z = (1 + 2 + 4)/3 = 7/3. The tilted law is (1/3)(1, 2, 4)/(7/3) = (1/7, 2/7, 4/7). I recomputed both with exact fractions.
(0 · 1 + 1 · 2 + 2 · 4)/7 = 10/7. So the mean energy of ν* is 10/7, and ν* lies on the boundary of A.
log(ν*(ε)/µ(ε)) = ε log 2 − log(7/3), so H(ν|µ) = H(ν|ν*) + m(ν) log 2 − log(7/3) is correct. For ν in A both corrections are nonnegative. Equality needs H(ν|ν*) = 0, so ν = ν*.

(10/7) log 2 + log 3 − log 7 = 0.14291, so ≈ 0.1429 is correct. The set A without the open ball is compact, and H is continuous on it, so its infimum is larger than I. Thus the conditional probability goes to 0.

review.why: All 6 outline steps are correct, and the cited proof supplies each of them. All 5 application steps are correct. The Ising ring example gives Λ*(4/5) = (4/5) log 2 − log(7/5) ≈ 0.2180. I checked the transfer-matrix trace for N = 12 and the Legendre transform numerically.

step_reviews.why: Hölder's inequality makes each log moment function convex, and the limit stays convex with Λ(0) = 0. The argument for Λ > −∞ and the bound Λ*(x) ≥ δ|x| − C are the proof of Lemma 4.4. The bound needs a closed ball in int D_Λ. This is a small point of the text, not an error.

A vector λ_x with the value min(Λ*(x) − δ, 1/δ) exists for every x. The exponential Chebyshev bound on A_x is correct, and a finite cover of K gives the bound. Since inf_K min(Λ* − δ, 1/δ) = min(inf_K Λ* − δ, 1/δ), the limit δ → 0 gives −inf_K Λ*.

The condition 0 ∈ int D_Λ gives Λ(±δe_i) < ∞. The 2d tail bounds and the principle of the largest term give the exponent −δM + max_i max(Λ(δe_i), Λ(−δe_i)). Step s2 on F ∩ [−M, M]^d then gives the bound for closed F, as on pp. 37-38.

Λ(η) is finite, so E e^(N⟨η, X_N⟩) is finite for large N and µ̃_N is a probability measure. The change of measure and ⟨η, z⟩ ≤ ⟨η, y⟩ + |η|δ on B_δ(y) give the bound. The inequality Λ(η) − ⟨η, y⟩ ≥ −Λ*(y) follows from the definition of Λ*.

The formulas Λ̃(λ) = Λ(λ + η) − Λ(η) and Λ̃*(x) = Λ*(x) − ⟨η, x⟩ + Λ(η) are correct. Λ̃ satisfies the hypotheses, because a ball around η lies in int D_Λ. Exposedness gives Λ̃*(x₀) > 0, so µ̃_N(B_δ(y)) → 1. The record writes η where the source has the typo λ.

For a lower semicontinuous, essentially smooth convex Λ, the set ri(D_Λ*) lies in 𝓔 (Rockafellar, and Dembo-Zeitouni Lemma 2.3.12). With y in D_Λ* and z in ri(D_Λ*), the point tz + (1 − t)y is in ri(D_Λ*) for t in (0, 1]. Convexity of Λ* then makes the two infima equal.

computation_reviews.why: D_Λ = ℝ and Λ is differentiable, so part (c) applies. From ρ_+ I derived Λ′(λ) = sinh λ / (sinh² λ + e^(−4β))^(1/2). A numerical derivative at λ = log 2 agreed.
At h = 0 the square root is e^(−β), so ρ_+(0) = e^β + e^(−β). The value is 4/3 + 3/4 = 25/12, which is correct.
cosh(log 2) = 5/4 and sinh(log 2) = 3/4. Then e^β cosh λ = 5/3 and the root is (1 + 9/16)^(1/2) = 5/4, so ρ_+ = 35/12. A full trace for N = 12 spins agreed with ρ_+^N + ρ_−^N.

step_reviews.why: The set G = {H > H(x) − δ} is open and contains x, because H is continuous. The lower bound of the principle gives liminf N⁻¹ log µ_N(G) ≥ −I(x). The limit δ → 0 and the supremum over x give the lower bound.

The closed balls give I ≥ I(x_i) − δ and H ≤ H(x_i) + δ. The complement C of the open balls is closed, and I > α on C. The upper bound on k + 1 closed sets and the principle of the largest term give the bound. The limits δ → 0 and α → ∞ finish the step.

H_M = min(H, M) is continuous and bounded by M, so step s2 applies to it. The split of the integral at {H ≥ M} is correct. Since T_M → −∞, the limsup is at most sup_E (H − I), and step s1 gives the limit.
Hölder's inequality with γ and γ/(γ − 1) and Markov's inequality give the bound e^(−(γ − 1)NM) ∫ e^(γNH) dµ_N. So T_M ≤ C − (γ − 1)M → −∞. If H ≤ M₀, the tail integral is 0 for M > M₀.

The upper bound with A = E gives inf_E I = 0. The compact level set {I ≤ 1} contains a minimizer x₀ with I(x₀) = 0, so sup (H − I) ≥ H(x₀). Steps s1 and s3 give sup (H − I) ≤ max(M, T_M), which is finite for large M.

computation_reviews.why: Under the uniform law, Z_N(β) = 2^N E exp(N H(M_N)). Cramér's theorem gives the principle with the stated I. The tail condition holds because |M_N| ≤ 1. So the lemma gives log 2 + sup g.

I′(m) = artanh(m), so g′(m) = βm − artanh(m). The function tanh(βm) − m is concave on [0, 1], has slope β − 1 > 0 at 0 and is negative at 1. So g′ > 0 on (0, m*) and g′ < 0 on (m*, 1), and g has its maximum at ±m*.
βm = (5/3)(3/5) log 2 = log 2, and tanh(log 2) = (4 − 1)/(4 + 1) = 3/5. So m = 3/5 solves m = tanh(βm). I recomputed this with exact fractions.

step_reviews.why: The path density is correct. Each stay at σ of length s gives e^(−r(σ)s), and each jump with label i gives the rate k^(i). The weight e^(−λ_i w^(i)) turns k^(i)(σ, σ′) into k^(i)(σ, σ′)^(1−λ_i) k^(i)(σ′, σ)^(λ_i). The Dyson series has the same nonnegative terms, and monotone convergence over n gives (5.2) of the source.

L_λ(σ, σ′) > 0 exactly when some k^(i)(σ, σ′) > 0, because (A3) then gives k^(i)(σ′, σ) > 0. So M = L_λ + aI is nonnegative and irreducible. Perron-Frobenius gives a simple root ρ with a positive eigenvector, and each real eigenvalue is at most ρ. This is the argument on p. 18 of the source.

e^(tL_λ) = e^(−ta)e^(tM) has nonnegative entries, so the entrywise bounds v/v_max ≤ 1 ≤ v/v_min stay true after the matrix acts. This gives (5.3) of the source. Since (ν, v) > 0, the limit is e(λ) for every initial law ν.

I checked L_{1−λ}(σ′, σ) = Σ_i k^(i)(σ′, σ)^(λ_i) k^(i)(σ, σ′)^(1−λ_i) = L_λ(σ, σ′). The label sets agree by (A3). So L_λ is the transpose of L_{1−λ}, as on p. 19 of the source. A matrix and its transpose have the same spectrum, so e(1 − λ) = e(λ).
The map λ = 1 − µ is a bijection of ℝ^m. With part (b), e(1 − µ) + ⟨1 − µ, z⟩ = e(µ) − ⟨µ, z⟩ + Σ_i z_i. The supremum over µ gives I(−z) = I(z) + Σ_i z_i, also when both sides are +∞.

The entries of L_λ are sums of exponentials in λ, so p(λ, x) is smooth. The Perron root is algebraically simple, so ∂p/∂x ≠ 0 and the implicit function theorem gives a smooth real root. The other eigenvalues have real part below x_0, because |μ| ≤ ρ and μ ≠ ρ. Continuity of roots then makes x(λ) the largest real eigenvalue near λ_0.

Λ(λ) = −e(−λ) is finite on ℝ^m and differentiable by s6. So 0 is interior to D_Λ = ℝ^m, the boundary condition is empty and Λ is continuous. Gärtner-Ellis part (c) applies along each sequence t_n → ∞, with rate sup_λ (⟨λ, z⟩ + e(−λ)) = I(z). The sequence argument correctly gives the bounds as t → ∞.

computation_reviews.why: The ring has rate 2 forward and rate 1 backward, so r = 3. L_λ has entries 2^(1−λ) forward and 2^λ backward, and each row sums to 2^(1−λ) + 2^λ − 3. A positive eigenvector of an irreducible nonnegative matrix is the Perron vector. So e(λ) = 3 − 2^(1−λ) − 2^λ, which is symmetric under λ ↦ 1 − λ.

e(−1) = 3 − 4 − 1/2 = −3/2 and e(2) = 3 − 1/2 − 4 = −3/2. Also e′(λ) = (log 2)(2^(1−λ) − 2^λ), so e′(0) = log 2. This is Λ′(0), the mean rate of W(t)/t, and it equals log 2 times the net drift 2 − 1 = 1.

e″(λ) = −(log 2)²(2^(1−λ) + 2^λ) < 0, so the supremum is at e′(λ) = z. At λ = −1, 2² − 2^(−1) = 7/2, which matches z/log 2. Then I(z) = e(−1) + z = (7/2) log 2 − 3/2 = 0.92602. A grid maximization gave the same value.

nm:statphys-kolmogorov-reversibility-cri.why: Source claim: Durrett Theorem 5.5.6 states the criterion for an irreducible chain on a countable set. Durrett proves both directions on p. 302. The record has no use evidence, so I judged influence and application from the mathematics. Inference: the criterion tests detailed balance without a guess for μ, and physics uses the loop ratio for entropy production. The proof uses only products along paths, so pro is 4.

review.conditions: The statement needs a countable S and an irreducible p. Condition (ii) applies to every loop whose reverse steps have positive probability. With (i), this is the same as the ratio condition of the source. The record adds positivity, uniqueness and the normalized case, and the proof covers all 3.
review.prerequisites: The Chapman-Kolmogorov equation (nm:chapman-kolmogorov-equation) writes p^n(x, y) as a sum over paths. This gives the paths with positive steps that s1 and s3 need. The other steps need only algebra, so no prerequisite is missing.
review.alignment: I read p. 302 of the local copy. Theorem 5.5.6 has the same hypotheses and the same conditions (i) and (ii). The source proof sets μ(a) = 1 and defines μ by path ratios, as in s3 and s4. The alignment honestly says that the record adds uniqueness, positivity and the normalized case.
review.why: All 5 steps are correct. Step s3 correctly shows that the path weight does not depend on the path, which the source states in 1 sentence. All 5 application steps are correct. The loop ratio is (2/3)³/(1/3)³ = 8, and the edge current is 1/9.

step_reviews.why: Irreducibility and Chapman-Kolmogorov give a path with positive steps between any 2 states. Detailed balance with μ(u) > 0 and p(u, v) > 0 forces μ(v) > 0 and p(v, u) > 0. Induction along paths gives μ > 0 everywhere. The ratio ν/μ is constant along each positive step, so ν = cμ.

Step s1 gives (i). For a loop with positive reverse steps, (i) gives positive forward steps. Detailed balance with μ > 0 gives each ratio as μ(x_i)/μ(x_{i−1}). The product telescopes to 1, which is (ii), as in the source proof.

By (i), each admissible loop also has positive reverse steps, so (ii) applies to it. The weight is multiplicative, and the reversed path has weight 1/w. For admissible paths γ and γ′ from a to x, γ then the reverse of γ′ is an admissible loop of weight 1. So μ(x) = w(γ) is well defined in (0, ∞).

The extended path is admissible and has weight w(γ)p(x, y)/p(y, x). Step s3 gives μ(y) = μ(x)p(x, y)/p(y, x), which is detailed balance. If p(x, y) = 0, then (i) gives p(y, x) = 0, and both sides are 0.

The sum of the detailed balance equations over x is valid because all terms are nonnegative. It gives πp = π because each row of p sums to 1. Step s1 gives the uniqueness of the normalized reversible measure.

computation_reviews.why: The loop 0 → 1 → 2 → 0 has forward product p(0, 1)p(1, 2)p(2, 0) = (2/3)³ = 8/27. The backward product p(1, 0)p(2, 1)p(0, 2) is (1/3)³ = 1/27. All reverse steps have probability 1/3 > 0, so (ii) applies to this loop.
The ratio (8/27)/(1/27) = 8 is not 1, so (ii) fails. The hypotheses hold: the space is finite, the chain is irreducible and (i) holds. So the criterion correctly gives no reversible measure.

Column 0 has p(1, 0) + p(2, 0) = 1/3 + 2/3 = 1, and the other columns are the same by rotation. So p is doubly stochastic and the uniform law is stationary. By a2 this law cannot satisfy detailed balance.
J = (1/3)(2/3) − (1/3)(1/3) = 2/9 − 1/9 = 1/9. Detailed balance makes J = 0 on every edge of a reversible chain. So the current agrees with a2.

With both probabilities 1/2, the loop ratio is (1/2)³/(1/2)³ = 1, and the uniform law satisfies detailed balance. The value log 8 = 3 log 2 is the cycle affinity in units of k_B. This physical reading is standard.

The record has no use evidence, so I judged influence and application from the mathematics. Inference: the result proves that the Metropolis-Hastings sampler has the correct target law. This sampler is a main tool in statistics and computational physics, so res, pra and rea are 4. The proof is a direct computation of a symmetric minimum, so pro is 4.

review.conditions: The statement needs a countable X, π > 0 everywhere and a transition matrix Ψ. The convention a(x, y) = 0 when Ψ(x, y) = 0 makes P well defined. The irreducibility claim needs Ψ(x, y) > 0 exactly when Ψ(y, x) > 0, and the record states this condition.
review.prerequisites: The record lists no prerequisite results. The proof uses only the definition of P, a minimum identity and sums of nonnegative terms. No catalog result is necessary, so no prerequisite is missing.
review.alignment: I read (3.4) and (3.5) on p. 41 and Exercise 3.1 on p. 45 of the local copy. The source gives the same P for a finite X and gives no proof. The alignment honestly says that the record adds π > 0, the zero convention, a countable X, the path reversal and the irreducibility condition.
review.why: All 5 steps are correct. Step s2 checks both cases of the flow identity. In s5 the case x = y needs a return path through a neighbor, which is trivial when |X| ≥ 2. All 4 application steps are correct. I recomputed the acceptance probabilities 1/4, 1, 1, 1 and the wrong law (4/9, 4/9, 1/9).

step_reviews.why: For y ≠ x, 0 ≤ P(x, y) ≤ Ψ(x, y) because 0 ≤ a ≤ 1. So the off-diagonal row sum is at most 1, and P(x, x) lies in [0, 1]. The definition of P(x, x) makes each row sum to 1.
If Ψ(x, y) > 0, then c min{1, b/c} = min{c, b} for c > 0 and b ≥ 0. If Ψ(x, y) = 0, both sides are 0 because min{0, b} = 0. So π(x)P(x, y) = min{π(x)Ψ(x, y), π(y)Ψ(y, x)} for all x ≠ y.
The minimum is symmetric in x and y, so detailed balance holds. The sum over x of nonnegative terms is valid on a countable X. It gives πP = π because the rows of P sum to 1.

Under the start from π, the path probability is π(x₀) times the product of the steps. Repeated use of detailed balance moves π to x_n and reverses each factor. The result is the probability of the reversed path, so the 2 laws are equal.

With the support condition, Ψ(x, y) > 0 gives π(y)Ψ(y, x) > 0, so a(x, y) > 0 and P(x, y) > 0. A Ψ-path from x to y ≠ x without its loop steps is a P-path. For x = y, a step to a neighbor and back is a return path. The step omits this trivial case.

computation_reviews.why: π = (4/7, 2/7, 1/7) is the normalization of (1, 1/2, 1/4). a(0, 1) = (1/7)/(4/7) = 1/4 and a(1, 0) = min{1, 4} = 1. a(1, 2) = (1/7)/(1/7) = 1 and a(2, 1) = (1/7)/(1/7) = 1. Only ratios of π occur, so the normalization cancels.

The plain rule gives P(0, 1) = 1/2, P(1, 0) = 1/2, P(1, 2) = (1/2)(1/2) = 1/4 and P(2, 1) = 1. The birth-death ratios are 1 and 1/4, so the law is (4/9, 4/9, 1/9). This is not (4/7, 2/7, 1/7), so the Hastings factor is necessary.

review.conditions: The statement needs a start from μ, a reversible and ergodic μ, and f ∈ L²(μ) with mean 0 and σ_f² < ∞. Mean 0 also follows from σ_f² < ∞ under ergodicity. The supremum in ‖f‖²_{−1} runs over ψ in the domain of L, and the record leaves this implicit.
review.prerequisites: The spectral theorem (wd:Q1425077) and monotone convergence (wd:Q1153584) give s1. The linked spectral record is the matrix form, but its nLab evidence covers self-adjoint operators. Banach-Alaoglu (nm:sequential-banach-alaoglu-theorem) gives s3, and Slutsky (wd:Q643826) gives s6. review.why: All 6 outline steps are correct and follow Sections 9.3.1 to 9.3.5 of the source. Step s5 makes the constant 9 of the source bound explicit. All 5 application steps are correct. I recomputed σ_f² = 1/γ, D = v²/(2γ) = 200 μm²/s and the exact variance formula.

step_reviews.why: Stationarity gives Var A_f(t) = 2∫_0^t (t − s)⟨P_s f, f⟩ ds, as on p. 80. Reversibility gives ⟨P_s f, f⟩ = ‖P_{s/2} f‖² ≥ 0, so t⁻¹ Var A_f(t) increases to σ_f². The spectral theorem gives the Laplace transform ⟨f, (λ − L)⁻¹ f⟩. Monotone convergence and Lemma 9.3.4 give σ_f² = 2‖f‖²_{−1}.

The resolvent u_λ solves λu_λ − Lu_λ = f. The pairing with u_λ and the duality ⟨f, ψ⟩ ≤ ‖f‖_{−1}‖ψ‖_1 give both bounds. The record writes λ‖u_λ‖² with the square, which corrects a misprint on p. 85. The bound ‖Lu_λ‖_{−1} ≤ ‖u_λ‖_1 is also on p. 85.

The bounded family u_λ has a weakly convergent subsequence in H_1. Mazur's lemma and the Cauchy property of −Lv_n give ‖w‖²_1 = ⟨w, f⟩. The liminf chain gives norm convergence, so strong convergence and λ_n‖u_{λ_n}‖² → 0. The uniqueness of w uses λu_λ → 0 weakly in H_{−1}, as on p. 88.

Dynkin's formula for u_λ in the domain of L gives the martingale M_λ. The relation Lu_λ = λu_λ − f gives A_f = M_λ + ζ_λ exactly. The identity E M_λ(t)² = 2t‖u_λ‖²_1 is (9.3.4) of the source. Strong convergence in H_1 makes M_λ(t) Cauchy in L², and E M(1)² = 2‖w‖²_1 = σ_f².

Cauchy-Schwarz gives E(λ∫_0^t u_λ)² ≤ λ²t²‖u_λ‖², and stationarity bounds the 2 end terms by ‖u_λ‖². With λ = 1/t the bound is 9λ‖u_λ‖², which tends to 0 by s3. The martingale part gives 2‖u_{1/t} − w‖²_1 → 0. This is Proposition 9.3.2 of the source.

The remainder t^(−1/2)ζ(t) tends to 0 in L², so also in probability. Proposition 9.1.1 applies to M, which has stationary ergodic increments and E M(1)² = σ_f². Slutsky's theorem then gives t^(−1/2)A_f(t) ⇒ N(0, σ_f²).

computation_reviews.why: Lf(x) = γ(−x − x) = −2γf(x), so P_s f = e^(−2γs)f. Since f² = 1, ⟨P_s f, f⟩_μ = e^(−2γs), and σ_f² = 2∫_0^∞ e^(−2γs) ds = 1/γ. The hypotheses hold: μ is uniform, reversible and ergodic, and f is bounded with mean 0.
(λ − L)f = (λ + 2γ)f, so u_λ = f/(λ + 2γ). The limit w = f/(2γ) satisfies −Lw = f. Then 2⟨w, f⟩_μ = 2/(2γ) = 1/γ, which agrees with a1.
Since −Lw = f, M(t) = w(η_t) − w(η_0) + A_f(t) is the Dynkin martingale of w. The remainder w(η_0) − w(η_t) has absolute value at most 2/(2γ) = 1/γ. So t^(−1/2)ζ(t) → 0, and A_f(t)/√t ⇒ N(0, 1/γ).
X(t) = vA_f(t), so X(t)/√t ⇒ N(0, v²/γ). The variance 2Dt gives D = v²/(2γ). With v = 20 μm/s and γ = 1/s, D = 400/2 = 200 μm²/s, and the units are correct.
With a = 2γ, 2∫_0^t (t − s)e^(−as) ds = 2t/a − 2(1 − e^(−at))/a². Times v², this is (v²/γ)(t − (1 − e^(−2γt))/(2γ)). So Var X(t)/t → v²/γ = 400 = 2D, which matches the expected value.

review.conditions: The statement needs a finite state space with at least 2 states, irreducibility and reversibility. Irreducibility gives π > 0. So some single state has π(x) ≤ 1/2, and Φ⋆ is a minimum over a nonempty family. The restriction to nonempty S is necessary and correct. The statement is true as written.
review.prerequisites: Step s2 uses wd:Q1425077 for an orthonormal eigenbasis of the self-adjoint P on ℓ²(π). Step s2 also uses nm:parseval-s-identity in its finite orthonormal-basis form, but the linked record states the Fourier-series form. Step s6 uses nl:16121 for the split of the sum. No necessary prerequisite is absent.

I recomputed π, P, the spectrum and both bounds of the double well with exact fractions. The general barrier formula γ = Φ⋆ = ½e^(−βh) is also correct.

step_reviews.why: The expansion of ½∑Q(x, y)(f(x) − f(y))² gives ‖f‖²_π − ⟨Pf, f⟩_π, because the rows of P sum to 1 and π is stationary. The identity for (f(x) + f(y))² follows in the same way. The argument for π > 0 is correct.

P is self-adjoint and P1 = 1, so P maps the complement of 1 to itself. An orthonormal eigenbasis of that complement gives λ₂ as its largest eigenvalue. Parseval gives Var_π(f) and E(f) as sums, and 1 − λ_j ≥ γ for j ≥ 2.

E(1_S) = Q(S, S^c) follows from step s1 and the symmetry of Q. The variance π(S)π(S^c) is positive because π > 0 and S is nonempty. The factor π(S^c) ≥ 1/2 gives 2Q(S, S^c)/π(S), and the minimum gives γ ≤ 2Φ⋆.

Each set S_t is inside {ψ > 0}, so π(S_t) ≤ 1/2 and the definition of Φ⋆ applies. The 2 integrals in t are correct because ψ ≥ 0. The symmetry of Q turns the sum of positive parts into half the sum of absolute values.

Φ⋆ ≤ 1 because Q(S, S^c) ≤ π(S), so the case γ ≥ 1/2 is trivial. The pointwise bound (I − P)f ≤ γf holds in both cases, because P has nonnegative entries and f ≥ f₂. Multiplication by π(x)f(x) ≥ 0 and a sum give R ≤ γ.
Step s4 applies to ψ = f², because {f² > 0} = {f₂ > 0}. Cauchy–Schwarz and step s1 give Φ⋆‖f‖²_π ≤ (E(f)(2‖f‖²_π − E(f)))^(1/2). The algebra to Φ⋆² ≤ 2γ − γ² is correct, because 0 ≤ R ≤ γ < 1.

computation_reviews.why: I recomputed (8/17)(1/16) − (1/17)(1/2) = 1/34 − 1/34 = 0. The Metropolis rates are correct: P(1, 2) = (1/2)·(1/8) = 1/16 and P(2, 1) = 1/2. Detailed balance on {2, 3} is the same by symmetry.
Only the singletons have π(S) ≤ 1/2. Each set of 2 states has mass at least 9/17. Φ({1}) = Φ({3}) = 1/16 and Φ({2}) = 1. So Φ⋆ = 1/16 is correct.
I checked that P(1, 0, −1) = (15/16)(1, 0, −1). For (u, v, u), the equations λu = (15/16)u + v/16 and λv = u give 16λ² − 15λ − 1 = 0. The roots are 1 and −1/16, so γ = 1/16.

(1/16)²/2 = 1/512 and 2·(1/16) = 1/8, so 1/512 ≤ 1/16 ≤ 1/8 holds. For a general barrier with ε = e^(−βh), the same algebra gives λ₂ = 1 − ε/2 and Φ⋆ = ε/2. So γ = Φ⋆, and the lower bound ε²/8 has the wrong exponent.

review.why: All 5 proof steps are valid, and all 4 application steps are correct. Step s1 divides by π(x) and does not state π > 0. The convergence prerequisite of step s2 gives π > 0, so this is only a gap in presentation. I recomputed 60 log 2 ≈ 41.59 and 9 log 2 ≈ 6.24.

step_reviews.why: Detailed balance gives self-adjointness in ℓ²(π). The expansion 1_y = ∑_j π(y)f_j(y)f_j gives P^t(x, y) = π(y)∑_j λ_j^t f_j(x)f_j(y), as in (12.4) of the source. Parseval gives ∑_j f_j(x)² = 1/π(x). The division by π(x) needs π > 0, which the convergence prerequisite gives.
Each f_j with j ≥ 2 has mean 0. The convergence theorem gives λ_j^t f_j(x) → 0 at every x, and f_j(x) ≠ 0 for some x. So |λ_j| < 1, and this gives a simple eigenvalue 1 and λ⋆ < 1.

The bound ‖h‖²_π ≤ λ⋆^(2t)(1/π(x) − 1) is correct, because f₁ = 1. Cauchy–Schwarz with ∑π = 1 gives the ℓ¹ bound. The inequality 1 − 1/t_rel ≤ e^(−1/t_rel) and a logarithm give the stated integer bound.

The identity λ_j^t f(x) = ∑_y (P^t(x, y) − π(y))f(y) needs E_π f = 0, which holds. The bound by 2‖f‖_∞ d(t) is correct. The choice of x with |f(x)| = ‖f‖_∞ gives λ⋆^t ≤ 2d(t), as in (12.15) of the source.
The case λ⋆ = 0 is trivial. Otherwise log(1/λ⋆) > 0, and log u ≤ u − 1 with u = 1/λ⋆ gives log(1/λ⋆) ≤ (1 − λ⋆)/λ⋆. The rearrangement to (t_rel − 1) log(1/(2ε)) is correct.

computation_reviews.why: A new value at a site i in S gives f_S the conditional mean 0. A new value at a site outside S keeps f_S. So Pf_S = (1 − |S|/n)f_S. The 2^n functions f_S form a basis, so the spectrum is {1 − k/n}.
All eigenvalues 1 − k/n are in [0, 1], so λ⋆ = 1 − 1/10 = 9/10. Then t_rel = 1/(1/10) = 10. The chain is lazy, so no eigenvalue is near −1.

π_min = 2^(−10) gives ½ log(1/π_min) = 5 log 2, and ε = 1/4 gives log(1/(2ε)) = log 2. So the bound is ⌈60 log 2⌉ = ⌈41.59⌉ = 42. The expression in the record computes the coefficient 60 of log 2, which is correct.

9 log 2 ≈ 6.238, so the integer t_mix(1/4) is at least 7. The order ½ n log n agrees with the known cutoff of the lazy walk on the hypercube. This claim comes from the literature, not from this theorem.

step_reviews.why: Each edge gives βσ_iσ_j = β − 2β·1[σ_i ≠ σ_j], and a disagreement edge is exactly a dual edge of ∂M. The product of the 4 signs around a dual vertex is 1, so the degree is 0, 2 or 4. The fixed rule then splits ∂M into contours inside Q.

Along L the spin goes from −1 at the origin to +1 at (n + 1, 0), so the number of sign changes is odd. Each change is a transversal intersection at an edge midpoint. The parity form of the Jordan curve theorem puts 0 inside some contour.

Int(γ*) contains only sites of B(n), because γ* ⊂ Q. Only the edges dual to γ* change status under the flip, so ∂M loses exactly the edges of γ*. With a fixed rule the pairs at each dual vertex stay the same, and the injective map E gives the ratio bound 1.

The intersection with the positive half-axis puts the dual vertex (u − 1/2, 1/2) on γ*. The intersection on the negative side gives a width of at least u, so k ≥ 2u. At most 4·3^(k−1) paths start at a fixed vertex and never use an edge twice in a row, so (2/3)k3^k is correct.

The sum (2/3)∑_{k≥4} k x^k is correct. I checked the closed form x⁴(4 − 3x)/(1 − x)² by algebra and numerically. The global flip gives ⟨σ₀⟩⁻ = −⟨σ₀⟩⁺. At x = 1/2, δ = 5/12 < 1/2, and x ≤ 1/2 exactly when β ≥ (1/2) log 6.

computation_reviews.why: At β = (1/2) log 6, x = 3e^(−log 6) = 1/2. Then x⁴ = 1/16, 4 − 3x = 5/2 and (1 − x)² = 1/4. The hypothesis x < 1 holds.
(2/3)·(1/16)·(5/2)/(1/4) = (2/3)·(5/8) = 5/12. I recomputed this value with exact fractions. The bound holds for every n because δ does not depend on n.
1 − 2·(5/12) = 1/6, so ⟨σ₀⟩⁺ ≥ 1/6. The global flip gives ⟨σ₀⟩⁻ ≤ −1/6. Both values are correct.

δ increases with x, and x decreases with β, so 1 − 2δ ≥ 1/6 for every β ≥ (1/2) log 6 ≈ 0.896. The exact value β_c = (1/2) log(1 + √2) ≈ 0.4407 is correct. The ratio 0.896/0.4407 ≈ 2.03 agrees with the conclusion.

The product ω_A∏ω_C^(n_C) equals ∏ω_i^(m_i). The sum over ω factorizes, and each factor is 2 or 0. The coefficients K_C^(n_C)/n_C! are nonnegative, so ⟨ω_A⟩_K ≥ 0 for every nonnegative family K.
For independent copies ω and ω', E[ω_Aω'_B] = ⟨ω_A⟩_K⟨ω_B⟩_K. So E[ω_A(ω_B − ω'_B)] is the covariance of ω_A and ω_B. The multiplication by Z_K² gives the stated double sum.

The map (ω, ω') ↦ (ω, ω'') is a bijection, because ω_i² = 1. Then ω'_C = ω_Cω''_C, and the identities for ω_A(ω_B − ω'_B) and ω_C + ω'_C are correct. The relation ω_Aω_B = ω_{AΔB} completes the change of variables.

σ₁·σ₁σ₂ = σ₂, so the derivative is ⟨σ₂⟩ − ⟨σ₁⟩⟨σ₁σ₂⟩. This equals 15/19 − 225/361 = 60/361 > 0. A finite difference in J gives 0.16620, which agrees.

P meets S because S separates x from y. Every vertex of P before the first vertex u in S is outside S. So the initial part lies in V_{S,x} and has no edge between 2 sites of S. Thus C_u holds for some u, and the union bound gives the sum.

With A₁ = {x, y}, A₂ = ∅ and B = {x, u}, the new sources are {u}Δ{y} and {x, u}. The removal of the indicator only increases the sum, because all weights are nonnegative. Step s1 then gives ⟨σ_uσ_y⟩_G⟨σ_xσ_u⟩_{G_{S,x}}, and the sum over u gives the inequality.

The right side is 2·(1/2)·(10/17) = 10/17, and 8/17 ≤ 10/17 holds. The ratio (10/17)/(8/17) = 5/4 = 1 + t². The values are correct.

The space X with pointwise convergence is the projective limit of the spaces ℝ^{d|j|}. The Dawson–Gärtner theorem gives the good rate I_X as the supremum of I_j. This is step 2 of the source proof.
Jensen on each interval gives I_X ≤ I. The grid averages g^k converge to g at Lebesgue points, also for non-centered intervals. Fatou with the lower semicontinuous Λ* ≥ 0 gives I_X ≥ I.
Λ*(x) ≥ M|x| − C_M is correct for λ = Mx/|x|. All partition terms are nonnegative, so M Σ|Δf| − C_M δ ≤ I_X(f). The 2 choices of M and δ give absolute continuity.

Exponential tightness in C_0 with the supremum norm lets the principle move to the finer topology. C_0 is closed in L∞([0, 1]), so I = ∞ outside it. Exponential equivalence then transfers the principle to µ_N.

computation_reviews.why: For the standard normal law, Λ(λ) = λ²/2 is finite everywhere. Its transform is Λ*(x) = x²/2, with the maximizer λ = x. So I(h) = (1/2) ∫ ḣ² for AC paths with h(0) = 0.
Evaluation at a fixed time is continuous for the supremum norm. So F is closed and G is open, and G ⊂ E ⊂ F. The 2 bounds of the theorem apply.
Jensen on [0, 1/4] gives (1/8)(4u)² = 2u². Jensen on [1/4, 1] gives (3/8)((v − u)/(3/4))² = (2/3)(u − v)². The piecewise linear path gives equality.

The slopes are 2 on [0, 1/4] and −2/3 on [1/4, 1], and 1/2 − (2/3)(3/4) = 0. The paths with u = 1/2 + η and v = −η lie in G. So inf_G I = inf_F I = 2/3.

step_reviews.why: Mollification gives f_k in C_c^∞ with f_k → f and ∇f_k → ∇f uniformly on 1 ball. H⁻¹ is continuous on that ball, so both sides converge. The extreme value theorem gives m > 0 on |x| ≤ r + 2, and the Heine–Cantor theorem gives the modulus ω.

Put z = (x + y)/2 and h = x − z. Then ½(2δf(x) − V(x)) − ½V(y) = δf(z + h) − D(z, h) − V(z). F_δ is a supremum of continuous functions, so it is lower semicontinuous. The Prékopa–Leindler inequality with weights ½ then gives ∫e^(F_δ) dμ ≥ (∫e^(2δf) dμ)^(1/2).

For |z| ≥ r + 1 the points z + τh with τ ≥ 1 − 1/‖h‖ lie in B(0, r + 1). The integral of (1 − τ) over that interval is 1/(2‖h‖²), so D ≥ m/4 and F_δ(z) = 0 for δ < m/(4M₀). For |z| < r + 1, D ≥ mη²/2 holds both for η ≤ ‖h‖ ≤ 1 and for ‖h‖ > 1.

review.conditions: The LSI is assumed only for bounded C¹ functions with bounded gradient, which is weaker than the source hypothesis. F is Lipschitz with L > 0. The proof shows that F is integrable. The bounds hold for every real λ and every r ≥ 0.
review.prerequisites: The fundamental theorem of calculus gives the integration of K' in s1. Dominated convergence gives the limits in s2 and s3, and Fatou's lemma gives the limits in s3. step_reviews.why: g = e^(λG/2) is bounded with bounded gradient (λ/2)e^(λG/2)∇G, so the hypothesis applies. The identity Ent(e^(λG)) = λZ' − Z log Z is correct. Thus K' = (λZ' − Z log Z)/(λ²Z) ≤ CL²/2. K(0+) = E G, and integration from 0+ to λ gives the bound. The case λ < 0 follows from −G.

A Gaussian convolution of a bounded function is smooth and bounded. An average of translates of H is L-Lipschitz, and the directional derivative gives ‖∇H_ε‖ ≤ L. Jensen gives E‖Y‖ ≤ √(nε), so H_ε → H uniformly. Dominated convergence with the bound e^(|λ| sup|H|) passes the inequality to H.

The tail bound and the layer formula give Var(F_k) ≤ ∫ 4r e^(−r²/(2CL²)) dr = 4CL². For k ≥ m, {|F| ≤ m} ⊂ {|F_k| ≤ m}, so the 2 events meet. Thus |E F_k| < m + r₀ and sup E F_k² < ∞. Fatou gives E|F| < ∞, dominated convergence gives E F_k → E F, and Fatou on e^(λF_k) completes the step.

Markov's inequality on e^(λ(F − E F)) gives exp(−λr + Cλ²L²/2). The value λ = r/(CL²) gives the exponent −r²/(2CL²). For r = 0 the bound is 1 and is trivial. The same bound for −F and a union bound give the factor 2.

computation_reviews.why: ∂F/∂h_i = ⟨σ_i⟩ is a Gibbs average of values ±1, so it lies in [−1, 1]. Thus ‖∇F‖ ≤ √N. F is smooth because the sum is finite and positive. The mean value theorem then gives L = √N.
The standard Gaussian law on ℝ^N satisfies the hypothesis with C = 1 by the Gross inequality. Herbst gives 2exp(−r²/(2N)). The substitution r = Nt gives 2exp(−N²t²/(2N)) = 2exp(−Nt²/2).
I recomputed 400 · (1/4)²/2 = 25/2. Then 2e^(−12.5) = 7.453 · 10⁻⁶, which rounds to 7.5 · 10⁻⁶. The expected value 25/2 is correct.
The only input is the bound ‖∇F‖ ≤ √N, and it holds for every graph, every β and every N. Thus the bound does not depend on the phase of the model.

Accept. U*S^±_jU = e^(∓iθ_j)S^±_j follows from [S^z, S^±] = ±S^±. Each bond gets the phases e^(±iφ) with φ = 2π/L modulo 2π, also the bond (L, 1). The sum gives −2(1 − cos φ)h_j.
Accept. ‖h_j‖ ≤ |J|(‖S^x‖² + ‖S^y‖²) = 2S²|J|. With 1 − cos φ ≤ φ²/2 and φ = 2π/L the sum is at most 8π²S²|J|/L. The term ⟨U*Φ₀, HU*Φ₀⟩ is at least E_0.
Accept. The index shift gives TUT* = U exp(−2πiS^z_tot/L) exp(2πiS^z_1). For half-odd-integer S, exp(2πiS^z_1) = −1. With S^z_totΦ₀ = 0 this gives ⟨Φ₀, UΦ₀⟩ = −⟨Φ₀, UΦ₀⟩ = 0.
Accept. Φ₀ spans the eigenspace of E_0. The min-max principle then gives E_1 = min ⟨ψ, Hψ⟩ over unit vectors ψ ⊥ Φ₀. The unit vector Ψ = UΦ₀ is such a vector.

computation_reviews.why: Accept. 8 · (1/2)² = 2, so the bound is 2π²|J|/L = 2π²J/L because J > 0. The even ring is bipartite, and the Lieb–Mattis record gives a unique singlet ground state.
Accept. 2π²J/100 = π²J/50 ≈ 0.1974J. The value 0.197J is a correct rounded value.
Accept. The bound 2π²J/L tends to 0 as L → ∞. The text correctly limits the claim to the family of finite rings and says that the theorem does not identify the cause.

nm:statphys-kms-gibbs-finite-dimension.why: The theorem shows that in finite dimension only the Gibbs state satisfies the KMS condition. Source: Proposition 2.20 of Jakšić, Ogata, Pautrat and Pillet gives the algebraic form, and Naaijkens gives the strip form. Inference: it motivates the KMS definition of equilibrium for infinite systems. The packet has no use evidence, so I judged influence and application from the mathematics. The proof needs only linear algebra and a Schwarz reflection.

review.conditions: The statement needs a finite-dimensional K, a self-adjoint H and β > 0. The convention τ_z(B) = e^(izH)Be^(−izH) agrees with (2.23) of the source. With this convention the Gibbs state satisfies both forms of the KMS condition, and I checked this directly.
review.prerequisites: Cauchy's integral theorem, Morera's theorem and the identity theorem give what steps s3 and s4 use. Together they prove the Schwarz reflection across ℝ. Steps s1, s2 and s5 need only linear algebra and the cyclicity of the trace.
review.alignment: Proposition 2.20 on p. 53 and the condition (2.24) agree with forms (ii) and (iii). Definition 3.4.4 of Naaijkens on p. 74 gives form (i) with ħ = 1. The alignment text says honestly that steps s3 and s4 are an authored reflection argument.
review.why: Accept. The 5 steps prove (iii) ⇒ (ii), (iii) ⇒ (i), (i) ⇒ (ii) and (ii) ⇒ (iii), so all 3 forms are equivalent. Step s5 follows the cited proof. The 4 application steps are correct and give the populations 3/4 and 1/4.

step_reviews.why: Accept. The trace inner product gives ω(A) = tr(ρA). For a unit vector ψ, |ψ⟩⟨ψ| = P*P with P = |ψ⟩⟨ψ|, so ρ ≥ 0. In finite dimension e^(±izH) is entire, so G_{A,B} is entire, and τ_{iβ}(B) = e^(−βH)Be^(βH).

Accept. Cyclicity gives tr(e^(−βH)AB) = tr(Be^(−βH)A) = tr(e^(−βH)τ_{−iβ}(B)A), which is (ii) for ω_β. The entire function G_{A,B} satisfies the strip conditions of (i), because τ_{t+iβ}(B) = τ_{iβ}(τ_t(B)).

Accept. h = F − G vanishes on ℝ, so the reflection h̃(z) = conj(h(conj z)) is continuous on the open strip. Goursat triangles in each half and a limit ε → 0 for triangles that meet ℝ give zero integrals. Morera's theorem then makes h̃ holomorphic.

Accept. ℝ has accumulation points in the connected strip, so the identity theorem gives h̃ = 0. Continuity gives h = 0 on Im z = β. At t = 0 this is ω(Aτ_{iβ}(B)) = ω(BA), and the substitution B ↦ τ_{−iβ}(B) gives (ii).
Accept. With A = e^(βH)C, (ii) gives tr(XCB) = tr(XBC), and cyclicity gives tr([X, B]C) = 0. C = [X, B]* gives [X, B] = 0, so X is central and equals α1. This is the proof of Proposition 2.20.

computation_reviews.why: Accept. e^(−βH)|2⟩ = e^(−βε)|2⟩ and ⟨1|e^(βH) = ⟨1|, so τ_{iβ}(B) = e^(−βε)B. Aτ_{iβ}(B) = e^(−βε)|1⟩⟨1| and BA = |2⟩⟨2|. This gives e^(−βε)p_1 = p_2.
Accept. τ_{iβ}(|1⟩⟨2|) = e^(βε)|1⟩⟨2|, and BA = |1⟩⟨2|1⟩⟨1| = 0. So ω(|1⟩⟨2|) = 0. A state is Hermitian, so ω(|2⟩⟨1|) = 0 too.
Accept. p_1 + p_2 = ω(1) = 1 and p_2 = p_1/3 give p_1 = 1/(4/3) = 3/4. The arithmetic is correct.
Accept. p_2 = 1/4 and ω(H) = εp_2 = ε/4. The Gibbs weights are 1/Z = 3/4 and (1/3)/Z = 1/4 with Z = 4/3, so the values agree with ω_β.

step_reviews.why: Accept. H commutes with the total spin. N = |Λ| is even, so each total spin is an integer and each multiplet has 1 vector with S^z_tot = 0. A unique ground vector in that sector gives 1 ground multiplet.
Accept. For x ∈ A and y ∈ B, ε(x)ε(y) = −1, and the exchange of d and d† restores the sign of the hop. The interaction becomes U n_{x,↑} − U n_{x,↑}n_{x,↓}. The sector N_↓ = |Λ|/2 maps to itself.
Accept. In matrix form H′ acts as W ↦ KW + WK − UΣ_x L_x W L_x + (U|Λ|/2)W. K and L_x are real symmetric, so W ↦ W* commutes with H′. Eqs. (1.14)-(1.18) show that |W| has energy at most that of W.

Accept. Lemma 1 of Freericks on p. 13 proves that the configuration lattice is connected through single hops. Each link has the matrix element ±t_xy ≠ 0, so the product of projectors and K is not zero.

Accept. Π⊥ on both sides removes the K terms, and positivity gives W^(1/2)L_xΠ⊥ = 0. Then WKΠ⊥ = 0, so the range of W is invariant under K and every Π_X. Step s4 gives W > 0, and a singular combination W₁ + λW₂ gives a contradiction.

Accept. The S^z_tot = 0 sector has finite dimension, and its lowest eigenvalue is simple for every U > 0. So the Riesz projection P(U) is continuous. Tr(P(U)S_tot·S_tot) is continuous with values in a discrete set, so it is constant.

Accept. Tasaki eq. (5.2) gives J_xy = t_xy²/U + t_xy²/U = 2t_xy²/U, with a sum over ordered pairs. The Lieb–Mattis record gives spin ||A| − |B||/2 with a gap in the sector. For large U the ground vector of H(U) has this spin, and step s6 extends it to all U > 0.

computation_reviews.why: Accept. 16 unit cells give 16 corner sites and 2 · 16 = 32 edge sites. So |Λ| = 48, which is even, and N = 48.
Accept. Every hop joins an edge site and a corner site, and the periodic lattice is connected. With |A| = 32 and |B| = 16, S = (32 − 16)/2 = 8.
Accept. The ground level is 1 multiplet of spin 8, so its dimension is 2 · 8 + 1 = 17.
Accept. The largest S^z_tot in a spin-8 multiplet is 8. For 16 unit cells this is 8/16 = 1/2 for each cell.

The spectral theorem gives Σ = U diag(λ_m) Uᵀ with λ_m ≥ 0, also for a singular Σ. A = U diag(√λ_m) Uᵀ is symmetric with AAᵀ = Σ. Cramér–Wold shows that AZ and X have the same law.

X_i = Σ_m A_im Z_m and step s5 give E[X_i f(X)] = Σ_j (Σ_m A_im A_jm) E[∂_j f(X)]. The sum Σ_m A_im A_jm equals Σ_ij for every A with AAᵀ = Σ. The symmetry remark is not necessary, but the conclusion is correct.

βH(σ) is a sum of N(N − 1)/2 independent terms with variance β²/N, so its variance is β²(N − 1)/2. Thus log E Z_N = N log 2 + β²(N − 1)/4. The exact gap formula follows from step a3.

It applies to many Gaussian processes in probability and statistics, so rea is 3. The equal variance condition excludes many pairs of vectors, so hyp is 2. review.conditions: The statement needs equal variances E X_i² = E Y_i² and the increment order E(X_i − X_j)² ≤ E(Y_i − Y_j)². It permits singular covariances and dependent X and Y. review.why: All 6 proof steps and all 4 application steps are correct. The cutoff ψ(s) = 10s³ − 15s⁴ + 6s⁵ is C² with ψ′ ≥ 0, so ∂_ij f_m ≥ 0 for i ≠ j. The GREM numbers 1/3, 1/9 and 8/9 are correct, and 8/9 < 15/16 agrees with the lemma.

step_reviews.why: The conclusion depends only on the 2 laws, so independent copies are permitted. Z(u) is centered Gaussian with covariance uΣ^X + (1 − u)Σ^Y. Under equal variances the increment order is equivalent to Σ^X_ij ≥ Σ^Y_ij.
The chain rule gives the derivative of f(Z(u)) for 0 < u < 1. On [a, b] ⊂ (0, 1) it has an integrable bound, because the derivatives of f are bounded. So Φ′(u) is the expectation of this derivative.

Gaussian integration by parts for (X, Y) in ℝ²ⁿ with block covariance gives E[X_i F_i] = √u Σ_j Σ^X_ij E ∂_ij f. The factors 1/(2√u) and 1/(2√(1 − u)) give Φ′(u) = (1/2)Σ(Σ^X_ij − Σ^Y_ij)E ∂_ij f(Z(u)).
The diagonal terms vanish because Σ^X_ii = Σ^Y_ii. The other terms are products of Σ^X_ij − Σ^Y_ij ≥ 0 and E ∂_ij f ≥ 0. Continuity of Φ on [0, 1] and the mean value theorem give E f(X) ≥ E f(Y).

ψ(1) = 1, and ψ′ = 30s²(1 − s)² and ψ″ = 60s(1 − s)(1 − 2s) are 0 at 0 and 1. So ψ is C². Each h_m does not increase, so ∂_ij f_m ≥ 0. Pointwise convergence and dominated convergence give the tail bound.
|M| ≤ Σ|X_i| gives integrability. Tonelli gives E M as a difference of 2 tail integrals. Step s5 orders both integrands in the correct direction, so E M ≤ E M′.

computation_reviews.why: The GREM and REM vectors have unit variances, and the GREM covariances are at least the REM covariances 0. So Slepian's lemma applies. The same holds for −X and −Y, which gives the comparison of minima.
The 4 REM energies are independent N(0, 1), so P(max Y_ab < 0) = (1/2)⁴ = 1/16. Thus P(max Y_ab ≥ 0) = 15/16, which I recomputed.
For ρ = 1/2 the orthant probability is 1/4 + arcsin(ρ)/(2π) = 1/4 + 1/12 = 1/3. The sector angle π − arccos ρ = 2π/3 gives the same value. The 2 pairs are independent, as stated.
The 2 independent pairs give P(max X_ab < 0) = (1/3)² = 1/9. So P(max X_ab ≥ 0) = 8/9, which is less than 15/16. This agrees with the lemma at τ = 0.

max_{T_k} X increases to ‖M‖ by continuity and density. Monotone convergence applies to max_{T_k} X − X_(t_0) ≥ 0, and E X_(t_0) = 0. So E‖M‖ ≤ E‖g‖ + E‖h‖ ≤ √n + √m.

review.alignment: Chatterjee p. 8 has only the problem and the credit to Osterwalder and Seiler, not the theorem. The alignment text says this honestly and says that the original 1978 paper is not open. The authored statement with explicit constants is a correct theorem of the same type. The extra reference to Cao, Nissim and Sheffield Theorem 1.2 supports the U(N) case.
review.why: Accept. I checked every step and every constant. The bound |f| ≤ ε, the center charge rule ∂η = −ζC, the chain map argument and the count 2^M(2D²)^n are correct. The Kotecký–Preiss condition reduces to (d − 1)/(6(2d − 3)²) ≤ 1, which holds for d ≥ 2. The final constants agree with the statement.

step_reviews.why: Since |Re χ_σ| ≤ n_σ, both e^(β Re χ_σ) and c(β) lie in [e^(−βn_σ), e^(βn_σ)]. Thus 1 + f lies in [e^(−2βn_σ), e^(2βn_σ)] and |f| ≤ e^(2βn_σ) − 1. The mean of f is 0, f is a class function and f(U⁻¹) = f(U). The expansion of the product is correct.

Distinct components of S use disjoint link sets, so Fubini's theorem factors the integral. The split of S into Γ and the other components is a bijection. The other components contain no link of C and share no link with Γ. The bound |K(Γ)| ≤ d_ρ ε^|Γ| follows from |tr ρ| ≤ d_ρ.

Schur's lemma gives ρ(z) = ζ(z)I with ζ a nontrivial character of Z. The identity Σ_η conj(η(w)) = |Z|δ_{w,e} gives f = Σ_η f^η. The shift w′ = wz gives f^η(zU) = η(z)f^η(U). The Haar shift U_e → zU_e then gives the condition ∂η = −ζC.

I checked π∂ = ∂π. Take a (1,k) plaquette with k ≥ 3. Its 2 links in direction 1 project to 1 link with opposite signs, and its other links go to 0. The top square argument shows that a closed finite 2-chain on ℤ² is 0. Thus πη = −ζQ, and Γ has at least RT plaquettes.

A link lies in at most 2(d − 1) plaquettes, and a plaquette has at most 4(2d − 3) neighbors. The tree walk gives at most D^(2(n−1)) polymers. With D²eε ≤ 1/4 the sum is at most |γ*|. Single plaquettes of Γ and the squares next to C give |log Ξ(Γ) − log Ξ| ≤ |Γ| + |C|.

At most 2(d − 1)|C| plaquettes contain a link of C, and the count 2^M 2^n D^(2n) is correct. The geometric sum with δ ≤ 1/2 gives the factor 2. Also 2^M e^|C| = (16^(d−1)e²)^(R+T), and R + T ≤ 2RT for R, T ≥ 1. The bound does not depend on Λ, so it passes to limits.

computation_reviews.why: For d = 4, D = 4(8 − 3) = 20 and D² = 400. Also c₁ = 16³e² = 4096e², which is about 30266. I recomputed both values.
With n_σ = 3, ε = e^(6β) − 1 and δ = 2e · 400 · ε = 800eε. Then δ ≤ 1/2 gives β ≤ (1/6) log(1 + 1/(1600e)). I computed β₀ = 3.83 · 10^(−5), and δ(β₀) = 0.5.
With d_ρ = 3 the theorem gives |⟨W⟩| ≤ 6c₁^(R+T)δ^(RT). The logarithm divided by T gives the stated lower bound. The hypotheses hold: SU(3) is compact, its center has 3 elements and ρ(ωI) = ωI ≠ I.
As T → ∞, the terms (R/T) log c₁ and (1/T) log 6 go to 0. Thus V(R) ≥ R log(1/δ) − log c₁. I computed log c₁ = 10.3178. At δ = e^(−12), which is below 1/2, V(1) ≥ 1.68 > 0.

nm:statphys-bfs-dynkin-isomorphism.why: Source claim: Bauerschmidt, Brydges and Slade state Theorem 11.2.3 on p. 178. They use it in their chapter on self-avoiding walk and supersymmetry, and they cite [148] for its applications. The record has no use evidence, so I judged the other scores from the mathematics. Inference: the identity gives walk representations for spin models, so pra and rea are 3. The proof needs Gaussian integrals, a first jump equation and a uniqueness theorem for measures, so pro is 2.

review.conditions: The statement needs a finite set, a symmetric nonnegative β and a Borel F with |F(t)| ≤ Ce^(−εΣt). These are the conditions of Theorem 11.2.3. The added claim of absolute convergence is true by the bounds in step s4. The diagonal entries of β have no effect on Δ_β, so the statement can allow them.
review.prerequisites: Fubini and Tonelli cover the exchanges in steps s2, s3 and s4. The Stone–Weierstrass theorem gives the density in step s5. Step s5 uses the uniqueness part of Riesz–Markov–Kakutani for a finite signed measure. The catalog record states the positive functional form, but uniqueness for signed measures on a compact metric space is standard.
review.alignment: I read the local copy of arXiv:1907.05474. Theorem 11.2.3 on p. 178 matches the statement, and Exercise 11.2.1 and Lemma 11.2.2 on p. 176 give the definitions. The exercise assumes β̄_x > 0, and the authored proof also covers β̄_x = 0. The alignment text describes the changes in the proof honestly.
review.why: Accept. Every step is correct. The first jump equation gives AG = I directly. The two measures μ_L and μ_R have the same Laplace transform on [0, ∞)^Λ. The compact space [0, ∞]^Λ and Stone–Weierstrass then give μ_L = μ_R. The 2-site check gives 2π/(3√3) on both sides.

step_reviews.why: Symmetry of β gives (u, −Δ_β u) = ½Σβ_xy(u_x − u_y)² ≥ 0, so A = −Δ_β + V is positive definite. The identity (v, τ) = ½Σ_i(ϕ^i, Vϕ^i) is correct. The Gaussian integral gives (A⁻¹)_xy Z_A with Z_A = ((2π)^|Λ|/det A)^(n/2).

The first jump time σ is exponential with rate β̄_x and is independent of the jump target. Then E[(1 − e^(−v_xσ))/v_x] = 1/(β̄_x + v_x) and E[e^(−v_xσ)] = β̄_x/(β̄_x + v_x). The result (β̄_x + v_x)G(x, y) − Σβ_xz G(z, y) = δ_xy is AG = I.
For F = e^(−(v, t)) the walk factor separates from the field factor. The right integrand is not negative, so Tonelli applies. Both sides equal Z_A(A⁻¹)_xy by steps s1 and s2.

The bound |F| ≤ Ce^(−εΣt) gives the integrable majorant e^(−½(ϕ, (−Δ_β + ε)ϕ)) on the left. On the right, Σ_u L_{T,u} = T gives the extra factor e^(−εT). Both measures are finite. Their Laplace transforms at w ≥ 0 are the two sides for exponents w + δ > 0, so step s3 applies.

The map t ↦ e^(−t) makes [0, ∞]^Λ homeomorphic to [0, 1]^Λ. Each e_w extends continuously, the span is an algebra with constants, and the functions e^(−t_z) separate points. Stone–Weierstrass gives density, and uniqueness of finite signed Borel measures gives μ_L = μ_R.
H = Fe^(δΣt) is Borel and bounded by C, because δ = ε/2 < ε. The weight e^(−δΣ) in μ_L and μ_R cancels the factor e^(δΣ) in H. Thus ∫H dμ_L and ∫H dμ_R are the two sides for F, and they are equal.

computation_reviews.why: For β₁₂ = 1, −Δ_β has rows (1, −1) and (−1, 1). With F = e^(−t₁ − t₂), A = −Δ_β + I has rows (2, −1) and (−1, 2). Then det A = 3, (A⁻¹)₁₂ = 1/3 and Z_A = 2π/√3. The left side is 2π/(3√3).
The probability p(T) of the walk at site 2 satisfies p′ = (1 − p) − p = 1 − 2p with p(0) = 0. Thus p(T) = (1 − e^(−2T))/2. Since L_{T,1} + L_{T,2} = T, the factor is e^(−τ₁ − τ₂)e^(−T).
The integral ∫₀^∞ e^(−T)(1 − e^(−2T))/2 dT is ½(1 − 1/3) = 1/3, and a numerical integral agrees. The right side is (1/3)Z_A = 2π/(3√3), which equals the left side.
For g > 0 the function F is positive and e^(Σt)F(t) is bounded, so the theorem applies with ε = 1. On a connected graph P_x(X(T) = y) > 0 for T > 0. Thus the right side is strictly positive.
The left side divided by the positive normalization Z is ⟨ϕ_x^1 ϕ_y^1⟩ of the |ϕ|⁴ model. Step a4 shows that it is positive for all g > 0, real ν and n ≥ 1. The conclusion is correct.

nm:statphys-generalized-ray-knight.why: Source claim: Sabot and Tarrès state Theorem 1 on p. 2. They also say that it has a crucial role in the cover time work of Ding, Lee and Peres. It also has a role in random interlacements, so res is 4. The record has no other use evidence, so I judged pra and app from the mathematics. The proof needs a change of variables, a martingale and optional stopping, so pro is 2.

review.conditions: The statement needs a finite connected graph without loops, positive conductances, a start at x₀ and a field that is independent of X. These are the conditions of the source. The field has density proportional to exp(−E/2) with E over ordered pairs, and its covariance is g_U. The claim holds for each fixed u > 0.
review.prerequisites: Tonelli applies in steps s1 and s2 because the integrands are not negative. At X_T = x₀ the signs cancel, so M_T is positive there. The change of variables formula gives the Jacobian Π Φ_x/ϕ_x. Optional stopping needs a uniformly integrable martingale in continuous time. The catalog record has a discrete form, but the extension is standard.
review.alignment: I read the local copy of arXiv:1311.6622v2. Theorem 1 on p. 2 matches the statement, and p. 1 gives the same definitions. Section 2 on pp. 4-6 contains (2.1) to (2.8) and Lemmas 2 and 3. The record correctly gives the theorem to Eisenbaum, Kaspi, Marcus, Rosen and Shi.
review.why: Accept. The 5 outline steps follow the source proof in order, and each claim agrees with the source. I checked the derivative ∂E/∂ψ_x = −2Lψ(x) and the identity Lf/f = Lψ(X_t)/ψ_{X_t}. The record adds the reason for T < ∞, which is recurrence on a finite connected graph. The one-edge application is correct.

step_reviews.why: This is (2.1) of the source. The sign split ϕ = σ|ϕ| with σ_{x₀} = +1 turns the integral over ℝ^U into a sum of 2^|U| integrals over the positive quadrant. The constant C is the Gaussian normalization.

The map T_u and the set D_u agree with p. 4, and the Jacobian of the inverse map is Π_{x∈U} Φ_x/ϕ_x. The equivalence (2.4) holds because the first site with ℓ_i = Φ_i²/2 is x₀ exactly when T = τ_u. At T = τ_u, M_T gives the old integrand, so (2.6) follows.

Only Φ_{X_t}(t) moves, with derivative −1/Φ_{X_t}(t). With ∂E/∂ψ_x = −2Lψ(x), dE/dt = 2Lψ(X_t)/ψ_{X_t}, which equals 2(L̃f/f). This gives the martingale of Lemma 2. The source proves uniform integrability with the exponential variables m_j.
This is Lemma 3. At X_T = x ≠ x₀, Φ_x(T) = 0, so a flip of σ_x changes only the numerator factor σ_xΦ_x(0). Thus M_T changes sign, and the terms cancel in pairs.

T < ∞ almost surely because each local time on a finite connected graph goes to infinity. Optional stopping and Lemma 3 give E[N_T 1{X_T = x₀}] = N_0. The sum over σ restores the full integral. The Dirichlet form ignores a constant shift, so the substitution Φ = ϕ + √(2u) ends the proof.

computation_reviews.why: From x₀ the process jumps to x at rate W = 2 per unit of local time. Thus the number of visits to x before τ_u is Poisson with mean Wu = 6. Each visit lasts an exponential time with mean 1/2. The mean is 6 · 1/2 = 3 = u.
Here E(ϕ, ϕ) = Wϕ_x², so ϕ_x has variance s = 1/W = 1/2. Then E[(ϕ + √6)²/2] − E[ϕ²/2] = (1/2 + 6)/2 − 1/4 = 3. This agrees with step a1.
For a compound Poisson sum, E[e^(−λℓ)] = exp(−Wu(1 − W/(W + λ))) = exp(−Wuλ/(W + λ)). With W = 2, u = 3 and λ = 1 the exponent is 6/3 = 2.

The formula E[e^(−λ(ϕ + a)²/2)] = (1 + λs)^(−1/2) exp(−λa²/(2(1 + λs))) is correct. Independence lets the factor (1 + λs)^(−1/2) cancel. With a² = 6, s = 1/2 and λ = 1 the exponent is 6/3 = 2, as in step a3.

nm:statphys-le-jan-isomorphism.why: Source claim: Le Jan states Theorem 9 a) on p. 20 and calls it a version of Dynkin's isomorphism. Corollary 3 on p. 13 gives the Laplace transform for every α. The record has no use evidence, so I judged influence and application from the mathematics. Inference: the result is a base for later loop soup and free field work, so res is 3. The proof needs Feynman–Kac, a trace log series, analytic extension and Stone–Weierstrass, so pro is 2.

review.conditions: The statement needs a finite connected graph, symmetric conductances and a killing measure κ ≥ 0 that is not 0. Then M_λ − C is positive definite and G exists. The Laplace transform holds for every α > 0 and every χ ≥ 0. The identity in law is claimed only for α = 1/2, and this is correct.
review.prerequisites: Feynman–Kac gives the bridge formula in step s1. Fubini exchanges the sum and the t integral in step s2. The catalog identity theorem has 1 complex variable. The extension in χ reduces to it on each ray χ = sχ₀, so it is sufficient. The Stone–Weierstrass record fits step s5.
review.alignment: I read the local copy of arXiv:0802.2478v3. Proposition 2 on p. 12, Corollary 3 on p. 13 and Theorem 9 on p. 20 match the record. The statement omits part b) of Theorem 9, and the alignment text says so. The excerpt also quotes Remark a), which calls the result a version of Dynkin's isomorphism.
review.why: Accept. The 5 outline steps follow the source in order. I checked the trace series, the identity (I − P)⁻¹M_k = GM_χ and the Gaussian determinant. Step s5 gives a correct Stone–Weierstrass argument on the one-point compactification, which the source only sketches. The 2-site application is correct.

step_reviews.why: With k = χ/λ, ⟨l̂, χ⟩ = ∫k(l(s))ds. The Feynman–Kac formula for the chain with generator P − I gives [e^(t(P−I−M_k))]_{xx}. Division by λ_x gives the bridge formula. This is the Feynman–Kac display on p. 11 of the source, before Proposition 2.

The series Σ(1/n)[Tr((P − M_k)^n) − Tr(P^n)] follows from ∫t^(n−1)e^(−t)dt/n! = 1/n. P is self-adjoint in ℓ²(λ) with norm below 1, so the series converges for small χ. Since (I − P)⁻¹ = GM_λ, (I − P)⁻¹M_k = GM_χ. Analytic extension gives all χ ≥ 0.

Campbell's exponential formula for a Poisson process gives E exp(−ΣΦ(l)) = exp(−αµ(1 − e^(−Φ))). Step s2 gives the value, so the determinant formula follows. For χ = te_x it gives (1 + tG^{xx})^(−α), which is the gamma law.
φ has density proportional to exp(−½zᵀ(M_λ − C)z), and M_λ − C + M_χ is positive definite. The ratio of determinants gives det(I + GM_χ)^(−1/2). Sylvester's identity gives the symmetric form.

At α = 1/2 the Laplace transforms agree on [0, ∞)^X. The functions e^(−⟨z,χ⟩) with χ > 0 vanish at infinity, separate points and form an algebra with the constants. Stone–Weierstrass gives density, so the 2 laws agree on C_c functions and are equal.

computation_reviews.why: M_λ − C has rows (2, −1) and (−1, 2), and its determinant is 3. Thus G has rows (2/3, 1/3) and (1/3, 2/3). I checked the inverse.
det(I + GM_χ) = (1 + tG^{xx})(1 + sG^{yy}) − ts(G^{xy})². The mixed derivative of −α log of this at 0 is α(G^{xy})². For the log Laplace transform in −t and −s, this is the covariance.
By Wick's formula, E[φ_x²φ_y²] = G^{xx}G^{yy} + 2(G^{xy})². Thus Cov(φ_x², φ_y²) = 2(G^{xy})² and Cov(½φ_x², ½φ_y²) = ½(G^{xy})². This agrees with step a2 at α = 1/2.
The value ½ · (1/3)² = 1/18 is correct, and I recomputed it. The mean is αG^{xx} = ½ · 2/3 = 1/3, from the gamma law with shape α and scale G^{xx}.
